proposition_tested: P2.4 (explicit disclosure of data gaps/omissions) - regulatory requirement in a non-medical diligence report
observed_finding: The federal All Appropriate Inquiries rule requires the environmental professional's written report to include an opinion on conditions indicative of releases and an identification of data gaps that affect that ability; persons conducting the inquiry should identify data gaps, the sources consulted to address them, and comment on their significance; sampling may be conducted to address data gaps.
population_and_setting: US property acquirers seeking CERCLA landowner liability protections; environmental professionals
outcome_measured: Required report content
short_exact_excerpt: should identify such data gaps, identify the sources of information consulted to address such data gaps, and comment upon the significance of such data gaps
limitations: Shows a disclosure obligation only; no evidence on how users act on data-gap disclosures. ASTM E1527-21 text not accessed.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a legally recognized diligence report with mandatory 'what we could not check and why it matters' disclosure exists in property transactions and is commonly part of renewable-project site diligence (Phase I ESAs). Verify: whether lenders/IC members actually read and act on data-gap sections, and whether similar disclosure is used in technical/IE reports.
analyst_inference: Closest non-medical precedent for coverage/omission visibility (X4) being codified; relevant as design precedent, not effect evidence.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (recipient retains independent obligations regardless of advisor report quality)
observed_finding: Under the AAI rule, the user (the acquiring party) must itself conduct certain inquiries - environmental cleanup liens (if not otherwise obtained), its own specialized knowledge or experience, the relationship of purchase price to fair market value, and commonly known or reasonably ascertainable information - and may provide that information to the environmental professional.
population_and_setting: Same as above
outcome_measured: Allocation of inquiry duties between user and professional
short_exact_excerpt: Persons identified under § 312.1(b) must conduct the inquiries listed in paragraphs (a)(1) through (a)(4) below
limitations: Obligation, not observed practice.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: some diligence work is structurally assigned to the recipient (user-specific knowledge, price relationship), so it persists however good the advisor's report is. Verify: equivalent recipient-retained duties in renewable lending (e.g., credit policy checks, KYC, sponsor knowledge).
analyst_inference: Formal allocation of retained work (W1/W4) that an advisor product cannot remove; supports P1.1.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standardized lexicon/format makes outputs repeatable) - counterevidence on judgment variability
observed_finding: With the standardized BI-RADS lexicon and assessment categories, five breast radiologists showed only fair agreement on final assessment category (kappa 0.28) and slight agreement on mammographic mass density (kappa 0.18), though some ultrasound descriptors had substantial agreement (kappa 0.61-0.69).
population_and_setting: 94 biopsied breast lesions in 91 women; 5 radiologists; one US center
study_or_observation_method: Independent re-description and categorization; Cohen kappa; PPV against pathology
intervention_and_comparator: Standardized BI-RADS terminology (no comparator)
outcome_measured: Interobserver agreement; PPV of categories
quantitative_result: Final assessment kappa 0.28; mass density 0.18; calcification description 0.32; mass shape/margin 0.48; US orientation/shape/boundary 0.61/0.66/0.69. PPV: 4a 6/102 (6%), 4b 17/110 (15%), 4c 48/91 (53%), 5 71/78 (91%).
short_exact_excerpt: Fair agreement was obtained for final assessment category (kappa = 0.28).
limitations: Abstract only; enriched biopsy sample; older BI-RADS edition; authors characterize agreement as 'good'.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: standardizing the vocabulary and categories of a report does not standardize the judgment behind them; in diligence, a standard risk-rating scale may still yield inconsistent ratings across analysts. Verify: inter-analyst agreement on diligence risk ratings under a common template.
analyst_inference: Format repeatability (P5.1) is distinct from judgment repeatability; standard categories do make disagreement visible and comparable.

proposition_tested: P5.1 (standard templates adapted locally) and P2.2 (structured checklist reduces producer-side rework/omissions)
observed_finding: A head and neck CTA template built from RSNA informatics (RadReport) templates plus locally chosen critical findings to assess on all CTAs was associated with fewer attending revisions of residents' after-hours reports; authors attribute the reduction largely to typographical errors.
population_and_setting: Resident after-hours head and neck CTA reports at one academic center
study_or_observation_method: Baseline revision rate vs 2-month template availability period
intervention_and_comparator: Structured template (RSNA-based + local critical-findings list) vs unstructured dictation
outcome_measured: Proportion of resident reports revised by attending
quantitative_result: 10/41 (24%) unstructured vs 2/17 (12%) structured reports revised (~50% relative reduction); no p-value or CI reported in abstract.
short_exact_excerpt: The structured template was found to reduce revision rates by approximately 50% with 10/41 unstructured reports revised and 2/17 structured reports revised.
limitations: Tiny sample; no significance testing reported; revisions mostly immaterial (typographical); producer-side rework, not recipient clarification.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a published standard template is adopted only after local adaptation (adding institution-specific must-check items). Diligence analog: a standard coverage list plus client/asset-specific must-check items. Verify: proportion of template content that is local vs standard in diligence deliverables.
analyst_inference: Illustrates the 'standard core + local additions' customization pattern for RadReport; the rework effect is weak evidence. No direct study of recipient clarification calls was found (see search_log).

proposition_tested: P3.2 Integration/AI assistance shifts review effort elsewhere rather than removing it; P1.3 Rework due to inaccurate output is a major driver (inside-frontier arm of the same experiment)
observed_finding: In the pre-registered field experiment with 758 BCG consultants, for 18 realistic consulting tasks inside the AI capability frontier, consultants with GPT-4 access completed more tasks, faster, and with higher-rated quality than controls; below-average performers gained most. For one task deliberately designed to be outside the frontier, AI users were less likely to be correct.
population_and_setting: 758 BCG individual-contributor consultants (~7% of that level); realistic consulting tasks; producers of analysis, not recipients reviewing outside work
study_or_observation_method: Randomized assignment to no AI / GPT-4 / GPT-4 + prompt-engineering overview after a baseline task
intervention_and_comparator: GPT-4 access (with or without prompt overview) vs no AI access
outcome_measured: Task completion, time, human-graded quality (inside frontier); binary correctness (outside frontier)
quantitative_result: Inside frontier: 12.2% more tasks completed on average, 25.1% more quickly, >40% higher quality vs control; below-average performers +43%, above-average +17% vs own baseline. Outside frontier: correctness ~84.5% control vs 60% and 70% in AI conditions (average -19 percentage points).
source_locator: Abstract (p.1); Section 3.1 'Quality and Productivity Booster - Inside the Frontier'; Section 3.2 'Quality Disruptor - Outside the frontier' (correctness paragraph, Figure 7, Table 4) — HBS Working Paper 24-013 as hosted at mitsloan.mit.edu
short_exact_excerpt: consultants using AI were significantly more productive (they completed 12.2% more tasks on average, and completed tasks 25.1% more quickly), and produced significantly higher quality results
limitations: Producer-side use of AI by consultants on their own tasks, not recipients reviewing outside analysis. Quality graded by humans; outside-frontier task deliberately designed so that GPT-4 would give a plausible but wrong answer (Section 3.2), so the -19 pp result is a constructed stress test, not a prevalence estimate. Working-paper version (2023); published version (Organization Science) not checked.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism analog only: advisor-side AI can raise output volume/quality on in-frontier tasks while degrading correctness on tasks where the AI is plausibly wrong. For renewable-energy diligence, needs verification of which diligence tasks are inside vs outside the frontier and whether recipients can tell. Differences: consultants are producers; no client review step was measured.
analyst_inference: Added by the coordinator to correct selective reporting flagged by R2C-01: the register previously contained only the outside-frontier arm. Read together, the two arms imply that rework risk (W3) is task-dependent and hard for producers to see, rather than uniformly high.

proposition_tested: P2.2 Traceability/structured evidence preserves or improves detection of material errors/omissions (baseline condition: professional review of AI drafts WITHOUT any traceability); P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort rather than removing it
observed_finding: Practicing primary care physicians reviewing AI-drafted patient portal replies failed to sufficiently address most erroneous drafts; each of the 4 erroneous drafts was missed by 13-15 of 20 physicians and 7-9 sent it entirely unedited; only 1 physician addressed all four.
evidence_type: direct evidence (professional reviewers, observed behavior, simulation)
population_and_setting: 20 practicing PCPs (19 attendings, 1 resident; mean 14.75 years post-medical school) from 13 sites, Baltimore-Washington area; simulated patient portal inbox
study_or_observation_method: Cross-sectional simulation: 18 simulated messages each with a ChatGPT 4.0 draft reply that participants could edit; 4 drafts contained investigator-identified errors (2 objective inaccuracies, 2 potentially harmful omissions); binomial tests
intervention_and_comparator: All participants reviewed AI drafts; no unassisted or traceability comparison arm
outcome_measured: Number of participants who insufficiently addressed ('missed') each erroneous draft; number sending unedited; survey perceptions
quantitative_result: Misses per erroneous draft: typo 14/20 (70%), outdated advice 14/20 (70%), blood-clot omission 13/20 (65%), DKA omission 15/20 (75%); unedited sends 7-9/20 (35-45%); mean 2.67 of 4 erroneous drafts missed (66.6%); all binomial p<0.001 (adjusted alpha 0.0125)
source_locator: Results section and Table 2 (Europe PMC full text PMC12022076)
short_exact_excerpt: Each erroneous AI draft was “missed” by at least 13 participants (65%) and was submitted entirely unedited by at least seven participants (35%).
limitations: Simulation without chart context; only 4 erroneous items; errors not deliberately engineered; no comparator, so detection cannot be attributed to the AI draft vs task difficulty; single LLM.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: an accountable professional signs off on a draft produced by someone/something else under time pressure, and errors that are absent (omissions) or plausible are hard to see. Consequential differences: clinicians review short documents about single patients with immediate feedback loops; credit/IC reviewers review long, multi-source analyses with delayed consequences, more numeric derivation, and committee-level second review. Needs verification in a diligence setting with seeded errors.
analyst_inference: This is the best professional-reviewer baseline found for 'review an outside draft that looks fine': detection of seeded/identified errors was low even among experienced accountable physicians. It shows the size of the gap any traceability feature would need to close, but tests no traceability feature.

proposition_tested: P2.3 Explanations/citations increase trust/acceptance without improving error detection (here: favorable perception without explanations/citations)
observed_finding: The same physicians who missed most errors rated the AI drafts favorably: 95% found them helpful, 80% agreed they reduced cognitive workload, 90% agreed they trusted the tool, 75% believed them safe. Total time on the study varied from 15 to 126 minutes; participants edited a mean of 10.05 of 18 drafts.
evidence_type: direct evidence (stated perception vs observed behavior in same participants)
population_and_setting: Same as R3A-E01
study_or_observation_method: Post-task survey (6-point Likert) plus logged edits and total time
outcome_measured: Stated helpfulness, workload, trust, safety; total study time; number of drafts edited
quantitative_result: Helpful 19/20 (95%); reduced workload 16/20 (80%); trust 18/20 (90%); accurate 14/20 (70%); safe 15/20 (75%); time on study mean 49.50 min (SD 30.33, range 15.15-126); drafts edited mean 10.05/18 (SD 5.94, range 2-18)
source_locator: Results: participant characteristics paragraph and Survey Responses / Fig. 1
short_exact_excerpt: Participants varied greatly in both time they spent on the study (mean = 49.50 min, SD = 30.33, range = [15.15, 126]) and number of AI drafts that they edited
limitations: No per-item time and no unassisted baseline, so no review-time effect can be estimated; time-detection relationship not reported.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests that recipient satisfaction/stated workload relief is not a valid proxy for verification quality among accountable professionals; any diligence pilot should measure detection directly.
analyst_inference: Trust-detection divergence occurs even with no explanation or citation present, so P2.3's mechanism (overtrust) does not require citations; citations could add to or offset it - untested here.

proposition_tested: P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort elsewhere rather than removing it; P2.2 (baseline: unedited drafts' error content)
observed_finding: Assessing radiation oncologists judged that unedited GPT-4 drafts posed a risk of severe harm in 7.1% and death in 0.6% of survey responses, mostly from misjudging acuity; they also reported improved subjective efficiency in 76.9% of cases.
evidence_type: direct evidence (professional reviewers; subjective efficiency, judged harm)
population_and_setting: 6 board-certified attending radiation oncologists, Brigham and Women's Hospital, 2023; 100 GPT-4-generated simulated cancer patient messages
study_or_observation_method: Two-stage observational study: stage 1 manual replies; stage 2 editing GPT-4 drafts; surveys on quality, safety, helpfulness
intervention_and_comparator: LLM-assisted (edit GPT-4 draft) vs manual reply by the same physicians (fixed order)
outcome_measured: Physician-judged harm of unedited drafts; subjective efficiency; response length and content
quantitative_result: Severe harm risk 11/156 (7.1%) survey responses; death risk 1/156 (0.6%); subjective efficiency improved 120/156 (76.9%); manual reply 34 words vs LLM draft 169 and LLM-assisted 160 words (p<0.0001)
source_locator: Main text, results paragraph (Europe PMC author manuscript PMC11829255); appendix p 19 for harm categories (not reviewed)
short_exact_excerpt: It was felt by the assessing physicians that the LLM drafts posed a risk of severe harm in 11 (7·1%) of 156 survey responses, and death in one (0·6%) survey response.
limitations: Efficiency not timed; harm judgments by participants; did not report how many harmful drafts survived physician editing in the text reviewed.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: an accountable professional signs off on a draft produced by someone/something else under time pressure, and errors that are absent (omissions) or plausible are hard to see. Consequential differences: clinicians review short documents about single patients with immediate feedback loops; credit/IC reviewers review long, multi-source analyses with delayed consequences, more numeric derivation, and committee-level second review. Needs verification in a diligence setting with seeded errors.
analyst_inference: Perceived efficiency gains coexist with a non-trivial rate of harmful content in drafts; the study does not show whether reviewers caught it, so it cannot resolve the time-vs-detection trade-off.

proposition_tested: P3.3 Drafting/reformatting is separable from substantive judgment
observed_finding: Physicians' LLM-assisted replies converged on the LLM draft's clinical content rather than their own manual assessments: content was more similar to LLM drafts than to manual responses, and inter-physician agreement rose from kappa 0.10 to 0.52; drafts were less likely to direct urgent action. Authors interpret this as automation bias and anchoring.
evidence_type: direct evidence (observed content change among professionals)
population_and_setting: Same as R3A-E03
study_or_observation_method: Content coding of manual vs LLM-draft vs LLM-assisted responses
intervention_and_comparator: LLM-assisted vs manual responses
outcome_measured: Similarity of response content; inter-physician agreement
quantitative_result: LLM-assisted vs LLM draft content p=0.81 (no difference); LLM-assisted vs manual p<0.0001; mean Cohen's kappa 0.10 (manual) vs 0.52 (LLM-assisted)
source_locator: Main text results paragraph and Figure (response content comparisons)
short_exact_excerpt: The content of the LLM-assisted responses were more similar to the LLM drafts (p=0·81) than to manual responses (p<0·0001; figure ).
limitations: Fixed order (manual first) and simulated scenarios; similarity measured by content categories.
transferability_to_target_workflow: If an advisor's draft is placed directly into the recipient's decision document, the recipient may adopt its substantive judgments rather than only its wording; integration may therefore not be a pure 'reformatting' saving (relevant to W1 vs W5 separation in IC memos).
analyst_inference: Evidence that 'drafting' assistance carries substantive judgment with it in a professional setting; challenges assuming drafting and judgment are cleanly separable.

proposition_tested: P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort rather than removing it / P2.2 detection preserved (here: less editing effort coincides with residual errors)
observed_finding: Blinded, time-constrained residents edited a smaller share of LLM-drafted hospital courses than physician-drafted ones and made less semantic change, but attending evaluators rated the edited LLM versions as having more confabulations (and more completeness); composite quality did not differ.
evidence_type: direct evidence (professional reviewers, effort and post-review error both measured, blinded to author)
population_and_setting: 10 internal medicine residents (editors) and 8 hospitalist attendings (evaluators), NYU Langone; 100 general medicine admissions (LOS 4-8 days), December 2023
study_or_observation_method: Quality-improvement study; residents blinded to author type edited each LLM/physician pair (10 min record review, 3 min editing); attendings rated edited pairs A/B on 4Cs
intervention_and_comparator: EHR-embedded LLM-drafted hospital course vs physician-written hospital course (both edited by residents)
outcome_measured: Percentage of characters edited (normalized Levenshtein), semantic change, attending ratings of completeness, concision, cohesion, confabulation
quantitative_result: Percent edited LLM 31.5% (SD 16.6) vs physician 44.8% (SD 20.0), P<.001; semantic change 2.4% (SD 1.6) vs 4.9% (SD 3.5), P<.001; completeness difference +3.00 (SD 5.28) favoring LLM, P<.001; confabulation difference -0.98 (SD 3.53) favoring physician, P=.002; composite +1.70 (SD 14.24) on 40-point scale, P=.46; no CIs reported
source_locator: Abstract Results (Europe PMC PMID 40802185); article results section
short_exact_excerpt: but with more confabulations (mean [SD], -0.98 [3.53]; P = .002)
limitations: Artificial time limits; confabulations rated comparatively after editing (no pre-edit error count, so catch rate unknown); convenience sample; single site; no provenance/traceability arm.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: an accountable professional signs off on a draft produced by someone/something else under time pressure, and errors that are absent (omissions) or plausible are hard to see. Consequential differences: clinicians review short documents about single patients with immediate feedback loops; credit/IC reviewers review long, multi-source analyses with delayed consequences, more numeric derivation, and committee-level second review. Needs verification in a diligence setting with seeded errors. Closest structural analogue found: reviewer improves a draft written by another author before it enters a formal record.
analyst_inference: The one professional study found that measures both editing effort and residual errors shows the effort reduction did NOT come with equivalent error removal: fewer edits, more surviving confabulations. Lower editing can reflect a better draft or less scrutiny; the design cannot separate these.

proposition_tested: P3.2 (qualifier: review time constraints and unfamiliar material limit detection)
observed_finding: Invited commentary on R3A-S03 states that LLM hospital courses continued to contain confabulations after human editing and that the 10-minute review window with unfamiliar patients may have limited residents' capacity to detect subtle errors.
population_and_setting: Commentary on NYU study (R3A-S03)
quantitative_result: Reports 32% vs 45% characters edited and 2% vs 5% semantic change (rounded from R3A-S03)
source_locator: Commentary text (JAMA Netw Open 2025;8(8):e2526350); excerpt seen via WebFetch extraction, not verified line-by-line
short_exact_excerpt: LLM HCs continued to contain confabulations even after editing by humans.
limitations: Same evidence group as R3A-S03; interpretation, not new data; excerpt obtained via an extraction tool.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Time-boxed review of unfamiliar material resembles a credit reviewer receiving a third-party report late in a deal; detection may depend on time allowed, which is the variable traceability would act on.
analyst_inference: Highlights that the review-time budget is a confounder: effort savings measured under fixed time caps say little about detection under realistic time.

proposition_tested: P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort rather than removing it (test: time and errors with seeded-error AI drafts)
observed_finding: Radiology readers editing AI-drafted chest CT reports (half with 1-3 seeded errors) were faster than when editing a normal template, with no statistically significant difference in clinically significant errors in final signed reports.
evidence_type: direct evidence (small crossover pilot, professional readers, seeded errors)
population_and_setting: 3 readers (1 radiologist, 2 radiology residents); 20 chest CT cases (CT-RATE); 59 signed reports
study_or_observation_method: Multi-case crossover; GPT-4-simulated draft reports with GPT-4-inserted errors in half; independent radiologist scored final reports; mixed models
intervention_and_comparator: Edit AI draft (platform highlights template insertions/positive findings) vs edit standard normal template
outcome_measured: Reporting time (case opening to signing); clinically significant errors in final report
quantitative_result: Median reporting time 573 s (IQR 403-895) vs 435 s (IQR 298-716) with AI draft, p=0.003 (24% reduction); clinically significant errors mean 0.27 (SD 0.52) AI-draft (n=30) vs 0.38 (SD 0.78) template (n=29), not significant; subgroup (drafts with vs without seeded errors) not significant
source_locator: Abstract; Results (Clinical Accuracy, Reporting Time, Subgroup Analysis); Table 1
short_exact_excerpt: The AI-assisted workflow significantly reduced average reporting time from 573 to 435 seconds (p=0.003), without a statistically significant difference in clinically significant errors between workflows.
limitations: n=3 readers, underpowered (null error difference is not evidence of equivalence); seeded-error catch rate not reported; simulated drafts; preprint.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Shows the study design needed (seeded errors + time + independent audit) but at pilot scale; image-to-text review differs from multi-document financial diligence.
analyst_inference: Weak counterevidence to the 'effort shifts and detection drops' pattern: time fell without detectable accuracy loss, but power is far too low to rule out meaningful misses of seeded errors.

proposition_tested: P3.2 (heterogeneity of time effect across professional reviewers)
observed_finding: Time effects varied by reader: two readers' mean times fell (717 to 398 s; 361 to 322 s) while one reader's mean time rose (947 to 1015 s); two of three said AI reporting required somewhat less mental effort.
population_and_setting: Same as R3A-E07
intervention_and_comparator: AI draft vs template
outcome_measured: Per-reader mean and median reporting time; survey
quantitative_result: Reader 1 mean 717->398 s; Reader 2 361->322 s; Reader 3 947->1015 s; medians 678->356, 354->312, 904->879 s; recommend scores 5, 9, 10 of 10
source_locator: Results: Reporting Time; User Experience; Figure 3
short_exact_excerpt: while Reader 3 showed an increase (947 to 1015 seconds)
limitations: Three readers only.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Reviewer-level heterogeneity suggests average time savings can mask reviewers who verify more thoroughly (and take longer) when given drafts.
analyst_inference: Consistent with the idea that some professionals treat a draft as something to verify (more time) and others as something to accept (less time); not testable here.

proposition_tested: P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort rather than removing it (field: time and audited accuracy)
observed_finding: In live clinical use, radiologists documenting plain radiographs with a workflow-integrated generative draft were faster than a matched baseline without the model, and peer review of 800 studies found no difference in clinical accuracy or textual quality.
population_and_setting: Radiologists at a tertiary academic health system (Northwestern); 23,960 radiographs (11,980 with and 11,980 without model); Nov 2023-Apr 2024
study_or_observation_method: Prospective cohort; linear mixed-effects model for documentation time; cumulative-link mixed model for peer-review Likert ratings
intervention_and_comparator: Model-assisted draft reports vs matched baseline set without model use
outcome_measured: Documentation time; peer-reviewed clinical accuracy and textual quality
quantitative_result: Mean (SE) 159.8 (27.0) s with model vs 189.2 (36.2) s without, P=.02 (15.5% efficiency increase); peer review n=800: clinical accuracy chi2=0.68, P=.41; textual quality chi2=3.62, P=.06
short_exact_excerpt: Interpretations with model assistance (mean [SE], 159.8 [27.0] seconds) were faster than the baseline set of those without (mean [SE], 189.2 [36.2] seconds) (P = .02), representing a 15.5% documentation efficiency increase.
limitations: Nonrandomized; peer review is a sampled quality rating, not a catch rate for model errors; developer-authored; abstract only.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Audited field evidence that an integrated draft can cut professional documentation time without detectable accuracy loss in a high-volume, short, standardized task; diligence reports are low-volume, long, and bespoke, so transfer is weak.
analyst_inference: Strongest field counterevidence to 'effort just shifts': time fell and audited accuracy held. It does not test provenance/traceability and concerns a task where the reviewer independently sees the primary evidence (the image).

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to sources/provenance reduces verification time/effort; P2.2 preserves accuracy (tested only as a bundle: LLM synthesis + per-claim citations vs EHR alone)
observed_finding: Clinicians completing realistic chart-synthesis tasks with a citation-first LLM tool (each claim linked to source record content via evidence cards) finished faster than with the EHR alone, with lower workload, and met prespecified non-inferiority for blinded-adjudicated accuracy, completeness and relevance.
evidence_type: direct evidence (randomized crossover, professionals, blinded outcome adjudication)
population_and_setting: 20 clinical staff (faculty physicians, trainees, APPs, others) across 7 specialties at Duke Health; 200 structured cases on charts unfamiliar to participants
study_or_observation_method: Two-period randomized crossover; log-transformed time in linear mixed model; non-inferiority margin -0.5 rubric points; senior physician blinded adjudication
intervention_and_comparator: Scout (LLM synthesis with per-claim citations and evidence cards; participants asked to verify in Scout or EHR) vs EHR-only
outcome_measured: Task completion time; NASA-TLX; accuracy, completeness, relevance (rubric)
quantitative_result: Geometric mean time 9.67 min (95% CI 8.29-11.28) EHR-only vs 6.03 min (95% CI 5.17-7.03) Scout; ratio 0.624 (95% CI 0.565-0.689), p<0.001; NASA-TLX raw 32.81 vs 24.07, difference -8.74 (95% CI -12.02 to -5.46); accuracy difference +0.20 (95% CI -0.20 to 0.61); completeness +0.84 (0.44 to 1.24); relevance +0.05 (-0.33 to 0.43)
source_locator: Results: Time Endpoint; Table 2; Output Quality and Figure 6 (arXiv 2604.26953 PDF, around p. 13)
short_exact_excerpt: This corresponded to a ratio of geometric means (Scout/Control) of 0.624 (95% CI, 0.565 to 0.689, p < 0.001)
limitations: Comparator lacks AI, so citations' contribution is not isolated; no seeded errors, so 'accuracy maintained' reflects whatever errors arose naturally; adjudicator authored the tasks; developer-authored preprint.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Closest professional analogue to an evidence-linked synthesis of a large record set (like a data room). Shows time can fall with accuracy held when claims link to sources; does not show the links themselves cause the saving or protect against plausible errors.
analyst_inference: Most direct professional RCT found involving traceability, but it answers 'LLM+citations vs manual search', not 'with vs without citations'. Treat as supporting the bundle, not P2.1 specifically.

proposition_tested: P3.2 Integration/AI assistance shifts review effort elsewhere rather than removing it
observed_finding: Authors state the tool shifts the core task from manual curation to verification; frustration did not significantly change (-3.36 points, Holm-adjusted p=0.192) and perceived performance slightly decreased, which they attribute to the cognitive cost of verification and reduced ownership.
evidence_type: direct evidence (subscale results) plus author interpretation
population_and_setting: Same as R3A-E10
intervention_and_comparator: Scout vs EHR-only
outcome_measured: NASA-TLX frustration and performance subscales
quantitative_result: Frustration difference -3.36 points, Holm-adjusted p=0.192 (not significant); other subscale values in Table 2 not fully extracted
source_locator: Results (NASA-TLX); Discussion paragraph beginning 'Scout and similar tools shift...'
short_exact_excerpt: Scout and similar tools shift the core task from manual curation to verification.
limitations: Interpretation by developers; subscale differences modest; brief training.
transferability_to_target_workflow: In diligence, evidence-linked outputs may convert reconstruction (W2) into verification work that remains and may feel less 'owned' by the accountable reviewer (W1).
analyst_inference: Even the most favorable professional study frames the residual work as verification, consistent with P3.2's shift (smaller, but not zero).

proposition_tested: P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort rather than removing it (field RCT: time vs self-reported accuracy)
observed_finding: In a three-arm pragmatic RCT, one ambient scribe (Nabla) reduced time-in-note by 9.5% versus usual care while the other (DAX) showed no significant change; clinicians reported clinically significant inaccuracies 'occasionally'; one mild adverse event was reported.
population_and_setting: 238 outpatient physicians, 14 specialties, UCLA Health; Nov 4 2024-Jan 3 2025; ~48,000 visits
study_or_observation_method: Parallel three-group pragmatic RCT, covariate-constrained randomization
intervention_and_comparator: Microsoft DAX Copilot or Nabla ambient scribe vs usual care
outcome_measured: Change in log writing time-in-note (primary); surveys incl. accuracy and safety items
quantitative_result: Nabla -9.5% time-in-note (95% CI -17.2% to -1.8%; P=0.02); DAX -1.7% (95% CI -9.4% to +5.9%; P=0.66); inaccuracies Likert DAX 2.7 (95% CI 2.4-3.0), Nabla 2.8 (95% CI 2.6-3.0) ('occasionally'); 1 grade 1 adverse event
short_exact_excerpt: clinically significant inaccuracies were noted "occasionally" on five-point Likert questions (DAX 2.7 [95% CI, 2.4 to 3.0]; Nabla 2.8 [95% CI, 2.6 to 3.0])
limitations: No independent audit of note errors or of whether physicians caught them; abstract only; short duration; usage ~30% of visits.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Product-dependent and modest effort reductions in a large professional RCT; error detection by the accountable signer was not measured, which is the same gap expected in diligence tooling evaluations.
analyst_inference: Large professional RCTs of drafting tools measure time well and detection poorly (self-report only); evidence on 'time saved while preserving error detection' remains unestablished even in the best-studied professional setting.

proposition_tested: P3.2 AI assistance shifts review effort rather than removing it (field RCT: time vs instrument-rated quality)
observed_finding: In a stepped-wedge pragmatic RCT, ambient AI reduced time spent on notes by 0.36 hours/day; PDSQI-9 documentation quality scores stayed high (3.97-4.99 of 5); diagnostic billing codes improved.
evidence_type: direct evidence (RCT, field); quality via rating instrument
population_and_setting: 66 health care practitioners, ambulatory clinics in two states (UW Health); 71,487 notes, 27,092 (38%) AI-generated; 24 weeks
study_or_observation_method: Stepped-wedge individually randomized pragmatic trial; linear mixed models, ITT
intervention_and_comparator: Ambient AI scribe vs pre-implementation usual documentation
outcome_measured: Time on notes; work outside work; PDSQI-9 quality; billing codes reviewed by professional coders
quantitative_result: Time on notes -0.36 h/day (95% CI -0.55 to -0.17); work outside work -0.50 h/day (95% CI -0.90 to -0.09; not robust to removing top 3% observations); PDSQI-9 means 3.97-4.99 across domains; billing codes improved P<0.001
source_locator: Abstract Results and Conclusions (Europe PMC PMC12858090)
short_exact_excerpt: Documentation time decreased without compromising diagnosis, billing compliance, or note quality.
limitations: PDSQI-9 is a quality rating on sampled notes, not a measure of omissions against the encounter or of clinician error detection; abstract only; no traceability manipulation.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Field RCT evidence that professional documentation effort can fall without detectable quality loss as measured by an instrument; the error-catching question remains unmeasured.
analyst_inference: Counterevidence to strong forms of P3.2 at the time level, but 'quality' here is not equivalent to detection of seeded/omitted facts.

proposition_tested: P1.3 Rework due to inaccurate/incomplete output drives review; P2.4 visibility into omissions matters for appropriate reliance
observed_finding: Two commercial ambient scribe products produced 127 errors in 31 of 44 draft notes (70%) from simulated encounters; omissions were the most frequent error type; authors argue omissions may be hardest for clinicians to identify because spotting them requires recall of the encounter.
evidence_type: direct evidence of error prevalence; author reasoning on detectability
population_and_setting: Simulated primary-care-type encounters read by 2 researchers acting as patients; 2 unnamed commercial ambient digital scribe products; MedStar Health
study_or_observation_method: Instrument validation study; error coding of draft notes
intervention_and_comparator: Product A vs product B (no human-review arm)
outcome_measured: Error count and type per draft note
quantitative_result: 127 errors (mean 2.9, SD 2.7 per note) in 31/44 notes (70%); omissions 55/66 (83%) of product A errors and 33/61 (54%) of product B errors; error type distribution differed (Fisher exact P=.002)
source_locator: Results and Table 1; Discussion (Europe PMC PMC11811668)
short_exact_excerpt: errors of omission were the most common; this error type may be the most difficult for clinicians to identify since the identification process requires memory recall of details from the patient encounter.
limitations: No clinician-review experiment; detectability of omissions is the authors' reasoning, not measured.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Omissions dominate AI-drafted professional documents; in diligence, unseen gaps (e.g., missing permit, unreviewed contract) cannot be caught from the draft alone - this is the case where coverage/scope visibility (X4) rather than citation (X3) would matter.
analyst_inference: Statement-level source links (X3) can only verify what is stated; omission errors require coverage visibility (X4). No professional study found tests X4 for omission detection.

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to sources/provenance reduces verification time/effort
observed_finding: A click-to-inspect interface linking each sentence of an AI-generated longitudinal patient summary to a matched source sentence was evaluated in a formative, qualitative usability study with clinicians; authors report feedback supporting sentence-level inspectability as a low-friction verification mechanism.
population_and_setting: Convenience sample of clinicians; remote moderated sessions Nov 2023-Jan 2024 (per search summary)
intervention_and_comparator: Sentence-level provenance interface vs (qualitative contrast with) document-level citation interfaces
outcome_measured: Qualitative feedback
source_locator: not located (abstract seen only via search-result summary)
limitations: No measured time or error detection in what was seen; access limited to search-result summary.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Design pattern (sentence-to-source links) maps directly onto evidence-linked diligence memos; the study supplies stated preference only.
analyst_inference: The most direct professional provenance-interface study located reports no quantitative verification outcome - an instance of absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

proposition_tested: P2.1 / P2.2 (deployment of statement-to-transcript linking without published outcome evaluation)
observed_finding: Per search-result summary of the vendor support article, Abridge's 'Linked Evidence' lets clinicians select note text to see the matching transcript passage and play the audio before signing. No evaluation of its effect on review time or error detection was found.
population_and_setting: Commercial ambient scribe deployed in US health systems
limitations: Access blocked; vendor claim; no outcomes.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Statement-to-source linking is already deployed in a professional sign-off workflow at scale, so an evaluation of its effect is feasible but none was found.
analyst_inference: Observed gap: the mechanism most analogous to evidence-linked advisor output is deployed in medicine, yet its effect on accountable reviewers' detection is not publicly tested.

proposition_tested: P2.1 Access to sources/provenance reduces verification time/effort (granularity of citation)
observed_finding: In an uncontrolled four-week pilot, equity research and compliance analysts strongly preferred table-cell-level citations over paragraph-level references, reporting verification 'in seconds rather than minutes'; explanations naming the specific source-vs-answer conflict were the most valued feature.
population_and_setting: 24 financial analysts (equity research and compliance) at one financial services firm; 1,847 queries over 43 SEC 10-K/10-Q filings
study_or_observation_method: Feasibility pilot with logging of analyst corrections and post-pilot Likert survey
intervention_and_comparator: FinGround claim verification with paragraph- and table-cell-level citations; no controlled comparator
outcome_measured: Self-reported design preferences; false positive/negative rates from analyst corrections; acceptability
quantitative_result: False positive rate 6.1% (analyst corrections); false negative rate 3.8% (27 analyst-flagged misses); 20/24 rated acceptability >=4/5 (mean 4.1, SD 0.7); override rate 5.8-6.3% across weeks (p=0.71 for trend)
source_locator: Section 6 'Deployment and Analyst Feedback'; Limitations; Ethical Considerations (arXiv 2604.23588)
short_exact_excerpt: table-cell-level citations (e.g., “Table 3, Row: Operating Income, Col: FY2024”) were strongly preferred over paragraph-level references, enabling verification in seconds rather than minutes
limitations: Self-reported, uncontrolled, single firm, developer-run with commercial affiliation; no time measurement.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Closest finance-domain evidence: analysts verifying AI statements against filings. Suggests citation granularity (cell vs paragraph) matters for verification effort - plausibly transferable to financial-model and data-room checks in credit diligence; needs controlled timing.
analyst_inference: Hypothesis-generating only: granularity of traceability, not merely its presence, may drive the effort saving.

proposition_tested: P2.5 Citations/traceability do not guarantee correctness or completeness; P2.2 (which errors evade professional reviewers)
observed_finding: Among 27 hallucinations missed by the system and flagged by analysts, 56% involved computational claims; authors state incorrect derived metrics are the most dangerous errors and hardest for humans to catch, warn of automation bias, and recommend mandatory human verification of numerical claims where small errors matter; a 'supported' label means consistency with the retrieved source, not correctness of the source.
population_and_setting: Same as R3A-E17; plus 50 near-miss adversarial claims
outcome_measured: Composition of missed hallucinations; detector recall on near-miss values
quantitative_result: 56% of 27 missed hallucinations computational; detector recall 71.4% (+/-6.3) on hallucinated values within +/-5% of ground truth
source_locator: Section 6 design insight (3); Limitations; Appendix 'Near-Miss Adversarial Analysis'
short_exact_excerpt: incorrect derived metrics are the most dangerous errors and hardest for humans to catch (56% of the 27 missed hallucinations involved computational claims).
limitations: Claim about human difficulty is not from a controlled human detection test; developer-run.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Renewable-energy credit diligence relies heavily on derived metrics (DSCR, P50/P90 yields, degradation-adjusted cash flows); a source link to an input does not verify a derived figure, so traceability must extend to calculations.
analyst_inference: Traceability to sources (X3) helps for extracted facts but not for computed claims, which are where professional reviewers reportedly miss most.

proposition_tested: P3.2 Integration/AI assistance shifts review effort elsewhere rather than removing it
observed_finding: Access to EHR-integrated GenAI-drafted replies for patient messages was associated with a 21.8% increase in physicians' message read time, no significant change in reply time, and 17.9% longer replies.
evidence_type: direct evidence (randomized waiting-list field QI study, professionals, logged time)
population_and_setting: 52 primary care physicians (25 immediate, 27 delayed activation) plus 70 contemporary controls; academic health system (UC San Diego), June-August 2023
study_or_observation_method: Randomized waiting-list design; mixed-effects models on EHR audit-log time
intervention_and_comparator: Access to GenAI-drafted replies vs no access (delayed group waiting period and contemporary controls)
outcome_measured: Time reading messages; time replying; reply length; likelihood to recommend
quantitative_result: Read time +21.8% (95% CI 5.2% to 41.0%; P=.008); reply time -5.9% (95% CI -16.6% to 6.2%; P=.33); reply length +17.9% (95% CI 10.1% to 26.2%; P<.001); median read time immediate group 26 s baseline vs 31 s at 3 and 6 weeks
short_exact_excerpt: The estimated association of GenAI was a 21.8% increase in read time (95% CI, 5.2% to 41.0%; P = .008), a -5.9% change in reply time (95% CI, -16.6% to 6.2%; P = .33)
limitations: No measure of draft accuracy or whether physicians caught errors; QI design; early tool version; abstract only.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Integrated drafts moved professional effort from writing to reading/reviewing without net time saving; a diligence analogue would be advisor content dropped into an IC memo template that the accountable reviewer must still read and check.
analyst_inference: Field evidence that integration can add review time rather than remove it; pairs with R3A-E01 (low detection) to show neither time nor detection automatically improves when drafts are integrated.

proposition_tested: P1.1 Retained review is substantially driven by formal obligations that persist regardless of advisor transparency (tests where the obligation stops for expert-made content).
observed_finding: Section 11(b)(3) sets two different defense standards for non-issuer defendants. For parts NOT made on an expert's authority, the defendant must show that 'after reasonable investigation' he had reasonable ground to believe and did believe the statements were true (b)(3)(A). For parts made on the authority of an expert other than himself, he need only show he 'had no reasonable ground to believe and did not believe' the statements were untrue or unfairly represented the expert's statement (b)(3)(C) — no affirmative investigation requirement is stated. Section 11(c) applies a single 'prudent man in the management of his own property' standard to both.
population_and_setting: US registered securities offerings; non-issuer defendants (directors, signers, underwriters); experts whose consent is filed (accountants, engineers, appraisers etc. per §11(a)(4))
intervention_and_comparator: Expertised vs non-expertised portions of a registration statement
outcome_measured: Legal standard for a due diligence / reliance defense
short_exact_excerpt: he had no reasonable ground to believe and did not believe, at the time such part of the registration statement became effective, that the statements therein were untrue
limitations: Statute states a standard, not how much work satisfies it; whether recipients actually skip re-performance for expertised content is not shown. US securities-specific; liability runs to investors, not to the recipient's own decision.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: the law itself draws the reliance line by WHO stands behind the content (a named expert who consents and is liable) rather than by how well documented the content is. In renewable-energy credit diligence, an independent engineer's or reserve/energy-yield consultant's report with a reliance letter is the closest analogue to 'expertised' content; sponsor-prepared models and summaries are analogous to non-expertised content. Consequential difference: lenders/investors are not under §11; their duty comes from credit policy, fiduciary duty and contract. Needs verification: whether credit policies explicitly distinguish expert-reported vs sponsor-reported items.
analyst_inference: The boundary between W1 (must investigate) and avoidable re-work (W2) is set by expert status plus absence of reasons to doubt, not by transparency. A traceable advisor product that is not 'expertised' (no accountable, consenting expert) would leave the recipient's investigation duty intact under this structure.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (tests what circumstances calibrate the required depth of independent investigation).
observed_finding: Rule 176 lists circumstances 'relevant' to whether a non-issuer conducted a reasonable investigation, including the type of issuer, security and person; the office held; other relationships to the issuer; '(f) Reasonable reliance on officers, employees, and others whose duties should have given them knowledge of the particular facts'; for underwriters, the type of underwriting arrangement, the person's role and 'the availability of information'; and responsibility for incorporated documents. It prescribes no procedures.
population_and_setting: US Securities Act §11 defendants other than the issuer
outcome_measured: Factors relevant to reasonableness of investigation
short_exact_excerpt: Reasonable reliance on officers, employees, and others whose duties should have given them knowledge of the particular facts
limitations: Non-exclusive list; no weighting; per R3B-S04 the SEC said only a court can decide reasonableness and a 1998 proposal to list practices (incl. comfort letters) was never finalized.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers as a pattern: the required depth of a recipient's own investigation is calibrated to its role, its access to information and the reliability of the people/reports it relies on. In renewable-energy deals this maps to lead arranger vs participant lender, or sponsor-equity vs passive tax-equity investor. Difference: no comparable rule codifies these factors for private credit; credit policies and interagency TPRM guidance (already in register) are the analogues. Verify: whether lender policies vary diligence depth by role/access in a documented way.
analyst_inference: Codifies that the W1 burden is role- and access-dependent rather than fixed; none of the factors is 'how transparent the advisor's output was', though 'availability of information' could be read to include it (inference, untested).

proposition_tested: P1.1 / P1.2 (where reliance without re-performance is legitimate vs where investigation is required).
observed_finding: The court held that only Peat, Marwick (the auditor) was an expert in the statutory sense and only its audited 1960 figures were 'expertised'; the company's and underwriters' lawyers who drafted the registration statement were not experts, so drafting by a professional did not expertise the document. Several outside directors and the underwriters were held entitled to rely on Peat, Marwick for the audited 1960 figures without investigating them, but not on management for the non-expertised portions, as to which each had to show a reasonable investigation (e.g., Auslander, Birnbaum, Grant; the lead underwriter Drexel failed as to portions 'not made on the authority of Peat, Marwick as an expert'; Coleman 'has not established his due diligence defense except as to the audited 1960 figures').
population_and_setting: Purchasers of BarChris 5½% debentures (1961 registration) v. directors, officers, underwriters and auditor; S.D.N.Y. bench trial
study_or_observation_method: Findings of fact and conclusions of law after trial
intervention_and_comparator: Expertised (audited) vs non-expertised (unaudited, narrative) portions; defendants with differing roles and knowledge
outcome_measured: Whether each defendant established due diligence / reliance defense
source_locator: 283 F. Supp. 643, section 'The "Due Diligence" Defenses' (preliminary matter on experts) and individual-defendant sections (Birnbaum, Auslander, Grant, 'The Underwriters and Coleman')
short_exact_excerpt: Neither the lawyer for the company nor the lawyer for the underwriters is an expert within the meaning of Section 11. The only expert, in the statutory sense, was Peat, Marwick
limitations: 1968 facts; single trial court; the court found that management misled several defendants, so holdings reflect an extreme fraud setting.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: a diligence report's legal 'weight' to the recipient comes from the accountable expert behind specific content, and only for that content. In an IC memo built on an IE report plus sponsor materials plus counsel's summaries, only the IE-certified portions are analogous to 'expertised'; counsel summaries are not. Verify: how lenders' credit memos label which content rests on which consultant's report.
analyst_inference: Directly locates the boundary: reliance without re-performance is legitimate for content certified by an accountable expert; everything else requires the recipient's own reasonable investigation, even if prepared by competent professionals. This limits how far a well-documented but non-expertised advisor product can remove W1 work.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (accountability for delegated investigation remains with the delegator) and P1.6 contrast (asking questions without verification is insufficient).
observed_finding: For non-expertised portions, the court held that asking management questions and accepting answers that would be satisfactory if true, without checking records, was not a reasonable investigation; 'reasonable investigation' requires more than accurately reporting 'data presented' by the company, and the extent of verification is 'a question of degree, a matter of judgment in each case'. The lead underwriter (Drexel) was bound by its counsel's failure to verify because it had delegated the factual examination of minutes and contracts to counsel as its agent.
population_and_setting: As above (underwriters and underwriters' counsel)
intervention_and_comparator: Questioning management only vs verifying against records
outcome_measured: Adequacy of underwriters' investigation
source_locator: 283 F. Supp. 643, section 'The Underwriters and Coleman'
short_exact_excerpt: is it sufficient to ask questions, to obtain answers which, if true, would be thought satisfactory, and to let it go at that, without seeking to ascertain from the records whether the answers in fact are true and complete ?
limitations: Concerns verification of an issuer's own representations, not of an independent expert's work; one court's judgment of degree.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers strongly to lender diligence on sponsor-supplied data (e.g., interconnection status, offtake terms, permits): a recipient that relies on summaries without tracing to source documents (minutes, contracts) is exposed. Traceability to originals (X3) is exactly what such checking needs. Difference: lenders' standard is contractual/regulatory, not §11. Verify: whether credit reviewers routinely trace sponsor representations to source documents and how long it takes.
analyst_inference: Supports the thesis mechanism that X3 traceability matters: the required check is 'ascertain from the records whether the answers in fact are true'. A product that links claims to the underlying records could lower the cost of that required step (W2) without removing it (W1). Also shows delegation does not transfer accountability: the delegator bears the delegate's failure.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (conditions that move the boundary: knowledge and role).
observed_finding: Reliance even on the expertised portion was unavailable to a defendant who knew facts indicating it was wrong: the CEO (Kircher), knowing the facts, 'had reason to believe that the expertised portion ... was in part incorrect'. Conversely, outside director Birnbaum was entitled to rely on Peat, Marwick because 'he had no personal knowledge of the company’s books'. The director who drafted the registration statement (Grant) was held to a higher standard of investigation than a director 'who had no connection with this work'.
population_and_setting: As above (individual directors/officers)
intervention_and_comparator: Defendants differing in knowledge and role
outcome_measured: Availability of reliance defense
short_exact_excerpt: He could not shut his eyes to the facts and rely on Peat, Marwick for that portion.
limitations: Fact-specific to insiders; the gradation by role is the court's judgment, not a formula.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: a recipient's own knowledge (e.g., a lender's prior exposure to the sponsor, internal portfolio data on similar projects) can defeat reliance on an expert report that conflicts with it, and staff closest to drafting the decision document carry more investigation burden. Verify: whether credit policies assign heavier verification to deal team vs credit approvers.
analyst_inference: The boundary moves with what the recipient knows: more knowledge (or more involvement) means less permitted reliance. This implies that integrating recipient-side data into the evaluation (RQ3) could increase, not decrease, the recipient's duty to reconcile conflicts.

proposition_tested: P2.4 / P2.5 (a documented scope/procedure list does not establish that the check was adequate or performed).
observed_finding: The auditor's S-1 (subsequent events) review followed a written program that the court found 'conformed to generally accepted auditing standards', but the senior accountant did not perform some prescribed steps, spent a little over two days, 'a total of 20½ hours' (CAP OCR text reads '20%'), found none of the material 1961 errors, and was 'too easily satisfied with glib answers'. The court held the review 'useless' as to results and the auditor failed its defense, while stating it was not requiring 'a complete audit'.
population_and_setting: Auditor (Peat, Marwick) as expert defendant; S-1 review of events after audited balance-sheet date
intervention_and_comparator: Written review program vs procedures actually performed
outcome_measured: Whether expert's own investigation was reasonable
quantitative_result: Review time reported by the court: a little over two days, 'a total of 20½ hours' (CAP OCR renders as '20% hours'); no material 1961 errors detected (court's finding). No comparator time given.
short_exact_excerpt: He did not take some of the steps which Peat, Marwick’s written program prescribed. He did not spend an adequate amount of time on a task of this magnitude.
limitations: OCR artefact in CAP text for the hours figure ('20%'); value read as 20½ from context ('a little over two days'). One engagement.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers to CL026-type 'procedures performed and findings, including none' disclosures by IEs or diligence advisors: a stated program and a 'no findings' result are not evidence that the procedures were carried out or were adequate for the risk. Verify: whether recipients of IE reports can check performance (e.g., site-visit logs, documents reviewed) rather than program descriptions.
analyst_inference: Qualifies the coverage-visibility thesis (P2.4): visibility of the planned checks (X4) differs from correctness of what was done (X5). A 'checks with no findings' list is only as reliable as the evidence that each check was performed; a court looked behind the program to what was done.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (red flags move the boundary on expertised content).
observed_finding: The court held that underwriters may rely on audited financial statements (expertised) under §11(b)(3)(C) but that reliance 'may not be blind': where red flags emerge, mere reliance on an audit is insufficient. For §11 a red flag is any information that strips the defendant of confidence in the accuracy of the expertised portion, whether or not it concerns accounting fraud; the 'prudent man' standard applies to (b)(3)(C); there is 'no category of information which can always be ignored'; and whether a red flag exists is an 'exquisitely fact intensive' jury question. Publicly available comparative data (WorldCom's E/R ratio vs competitors) could be a red flag even for audited figures.
population_and_setting: Bond purchasers v. underwriters (SSB, J.P. Morgan et al.) of WorldCom's 2000 and 2001 bond offerings; S.D.N.Y.
intervention_and_comparator: Audited (expertised) figures with vs without red flags
outcome_measured: Availability of reliance defense
source_locator: 346 F. Supp. 2d 628, Part III.E 'Case Law: Reliance Defense' and III.G.1 'Audited Financial Statements' (2000 and 2001 Registration Statements; E/R Ratio)
short_exact_excerpt: Any information that strips a defendant of his confidence in the accuracy of those portions of a registration statement premised on audited financial statements is a red flag, whether or not it relates to accounting fraud or an audit failure.
limitations: Summary-judgment ruling; jury never decided (settlement). Red-flag definition is one district court's formulation.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: a lender may rely on an IE's energy-yield or construction-cost conclusions until it encounters information (e.g., portfolio underperformance of similar sites, curtailment data, peer benchmarks) that undermines confidence; then a duty to inquire arises regardless of the IE's credentials. Difference: lenders face credit loss rather than investor suits. Verify: whether lenders document benchmark comparisons that act as red-flag screens.
analyst_inference: The legally relevant trigger for leaving 'reliance' mode is any confidence-undermining information, including public benchmarks. Structured evidence and explicit assumptions could make red flags easier to see (potentially increasing required W1 follow-up in some cases while reducing blind re-checking in others) — an inference, not shown.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (does disclosure of procedures performed + negative assurance shift what the recipient must do?) and P1.1.
observed_finding: The court held that auditors' comfort letters (SAS 72) and SAS 71 interim reviews are not 'expertised' statements: underwriters 'may not rely on an accountant’s comfort letters for interim financial statements' for the §11(b)(3)(C) reliance defense; comfort letters do not expertise non-expertised content. For interim financials the underwriters must prove their own reasonable investigation; receipt of comfort letters is 'important evidence' but 'insufficient by itself'. The court rejected the underwriters' request to rule that an investigation 'is reasonable when it rests on the independent auditor’s SAS 71 review', saying that would convert the due diligence defense into the reliance defense and balkanize (court: 'balkan-izes', OCR hyphenation) the task.
population_and_setting: As above
intervention_and_comparator: Comfort letter (procedures + negative assurance) vs audit opinion
outcome_measured: Whether comfort letter alone establishes underwriter due diligence
source_locator: 346 F. Supp. 2d 628, Part III.C 'Accountants as Experts' and III.G.2 'Interim Financial Statements'
short_exact_excerpt: In assessing the reasonableness of the investigation, their receipt of the comfort letters will be important evidence, but it is insufficient by itself to establish the defense.
limitations: District-court reasoning tied to SEC Rule 436 treatment of interim reviews; summary-judgment posture.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Directly relevant to CL026 in renewable-energy diligence: an advisor deliverable that lists procedures performed and findings (including none), without an accountable expert opinion, is evidence the recipient can cite for the reasonableness of its own process, but does not by itself discharge the recipient's investigation. Verify: whether lender credit policies treat 'agreed-upon procedures' style consultant outputs differently from IE opinions with reliance letters.
analyst_inference: Most direct answer to the CL026 question in this set: disclosure of procedures performed and findings changes the EVIDENCE available to the recipient (and probably the cost of its review) but not the legal LOCATION of the duty. Required recipient work persists (W1); what may be avoidable is re-performing the accountant's procedures (see next item).

proposition_tested: P1.2 (re-performance/reconstruction is not mandated; the required work is a reasonable investigation between reliance and re-audit).
observed_finding: Responding to the argument that denying reliance on comfort letters would force underwriters to hire accountants to 'rehash' the auditor's work, the court said nothing in the opinion imposes that obligation: underwriters 'are not being asked to duplicate the work of auditors, but to conduct a reasonable investigation'; reasonable investigation lies between obtaining comfort letters 'and doing little more' and re-auditing; if red flags arise, underwriters must inquire until satisfied and if unsatisfied 'demand disclosure, withdraw ... or bear the risk'; on aggressive accounting a prudent underwriter 'may choose to consult with accounting experts'.
population_and_setting: As above
intervention_and_comparator: Comfort-letter-only vs re-audit vs intermediate inquiry
outcome_measured: Scope of required underwriter investigation
source_locator: 346 F. Supp. 2d 628, Part III.G.2 'Interim Financial Statements' (closing paragraphs)
short_exact_excerpt: The term “reasonable investigation” encompasses many modes of inquiry between obtaining comfort letters from an auditor and doing little more, on one hand, and having to re-audit a company’s books on the other.
limitations: Doctrinal statement, not a specification of tasks; does not say how much time an intermediate investigation takes.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: lenders need not re-run an IE's energy model or re-perform a consultant's checks, but must ask the questions their own business expertise identifies and follow up on anomalies. Verify with lender workflow data: how much reviewer time goes to re-performing consultant work vs targeted inquiry.
analyst_inference: Explicitly separates mandatory W1 (targeted, judgment-driven inquiry; follow-up on red flags) from non-mandatory re-performance (re-audit). Re-performance that occurs without red flags is therefore not legally compelled in this setting — consistent with it being at least partly avoidable (W2) or driven by other motives (P1.6).

proposition_tested: P1.6 (review persists as record-building / defensibility rather than only marginal error detection).
observed_finding: The court stated that an underwriter must conduct a reasonable investigation to prevail even if the investigation would have proven futile in uncovering the fraud, and conversely prevails if it conducted a reasonable investigation even if no investigation would have uncovered the fraud. Lead Plaintiff's contentions (not findings) described the underwriters' diligence as a limited number of conversations, 'cursory' inquiries and failure 'to go behind any of the almost formulaic answers'.
population_and_setting: As above
outcome_measured: Whether process or outcome determines the defense
source_locator: 346 F. Supp. 2d 628, Part III.G.2 'Interim Financial Statements'
short_exact_excerpt: Conversely, an underwriter must conduct a reasonable investigation to prevail on the due diligence defense, even if it appears that such an investigation would have proven futile in uncovering the fraud.
limitations: Legal standard; the description of actual diligence is plaintiffs' characterization, not a finding.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: much lender and IC review is evaluated ex post by process (was a reasonable process followed and documented?) rather than by whether it would have caught the problem. A product that reduces effort must still leave the recipient with a defensible record of its own inquiry. Verify: whether credit-file requirements specify documentation of reviewer questions and responses.
analyst_inference: Review effort has a component whose value is the defensibility of the recipient's own process, independent of detection yield. This sustains W1 work even when advisor output is accurate and transparent; tools could help produce that record, but cannot replace the recipient's inquiry.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Legal doctrine on required investigation can diverge from effort actually expended (doctrine ≠ observed practice).
observed_finding: The opinion quotes academics and practitioners stating that, under shelf registration time constraints, 'serious due diligence efforts are simply not feasible' (Coffee, 1997), that disinterested advance due diligence is 'the exception not the rule' for shelf offerings (Partnoy, 2001), and an ABA committee letter to the SEC (2001) stating it 'is not possible' for underwriters to meet the standard in the current financing environment. The court nonetheless held the prudent-man standard has not been diluted by regulatory changes.
population_and_setting: US shelf-registered offerings c. 1990s-2001
outcome_measured: Feasibility of required diligence in practice
source_locator: 346 F. Supp. 2d 628, Part III.D 'Integrated Disclosure, Shelf Registration, and Rule 176'
short_exact_excerpt: It is not possible for underwriters and others to meet this standard in the current financing environment.
limitations: Secondhand quotations of opinion; no measurement of actual diligence effort.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers as a caution: competitive, time-compressed renewable-energy financings (portfolio deals, tax-equity closings) may similarly produce gaps between required and performed diligence. Legal standards therefore cannot be used to infer how much review lenders actually do. Verify: observed time budgets for credit review in competitive processes.
analyst_inference: Supports the coordinator's caveat that doctrine establishes required W1 work, not actual effort; it also suggests time pressure, not only transparency, constrains review.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (scope disclosure is designed to let the recipient judge sufficiency) and P1.1.
observed_finding: AS 6101 states that what constitutes a reasonable investigation of unaudited information 'has never been authoritatively established' and therefore 'only the underwriter can determine what is sufficient'; procedures short of an audit give accountants a basis for 'at the most, negative assurance'; such procedures do not provide assurance that accountants will become aware of all significant matters, so there is 'necessarily a risk' that negative assurance is given about the absence of conditions that existed. Any discussion of procedures must be accompanied by a statement that accountants cannot furnish assurance about the procedures' sufficiency for the underwriter's purposes.
population_and_setting: Auditors issuing comfort letters to underwriters in SEC-registered offerings
outcome_measured: Allocation of responsibility for sufficiency of procedures
source_locator: AS 6101.12 and .15 (compiled PCAOB standards PDF pp. 560-561)
short_exact_excerpt: What constitutes a reasonable investigation of unaudited financial information sufficient to satisfy an underwriter's purposes has never been authoritatively established. Consequently, only the underwriter can determine what is sufficient for his or her purposes.
limitations: Standard states allocation and rationale; it does not show whether underwriters actually exercise independent sufficiency judgment or accept customary letters.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: renewable-energy advisors (IE, insurance, market consultants) and their lender recipients face the same allocation — the producer describes what it did; the recipient decides whether that is enough for its credit purpose. Verify: whether IE engagement letters or reliance letters contain analogous sufficiency disclaimers (R3C may have scopes).
analyst_inference: The profession that produces the work explicitly refuses to own the sufficiency judgment; that judgment is a non-delegable W1 task for the recipient. Coverage visibility (X4) is the input to that judgment, not a substitute for it.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (visibility into checks performed, stated in unambiguous terms, as a design requirement).
observed_finding: AS 6101 requires the procedures to be 'clearly set out in the comfort letter, in both draft and final form' so the underwriter 'can decide whether the procedures performed are sufficient'; accountants should avoid statements that they carried out 'such procedures as they consider necessary'; terms of uncertain meaning ('general review, limited review, reconcile, check, or test') should not be used unless the procedures are described; the underwriter may request additional procedures and specify items and materiality thresholds, which must then be described; acceptance of the draft and final letter lets accountants assume the underwriter considers the procedures sufficient.
population_and_setting: As above
outcome_measured: Required content/wording of procedure descriptions
short_exact_excerpt: so that there will be no misunderstanding about the basis on which the accountants' comments have been made and so that the underwriter can decide whether the procedures performed are sufficient for his or her purposes.
limitations: Shows a mandated design feature and its rationale, not evidence that it reduces underwriter effort or improves detection.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers closely to CL026: a long-standing professional regime already requires producers to state procedures performed (and findings) in concrete, non-vague terms, specifically so the recipient can make its own sufficiency decision. Renewable diligence deliverables could be benchmarked against this (e.g., ban on undefined 'reviewed'/'checked'). Verify: whether IE reports in practice describe procedures at this specificity.
analyst_inference: This is the closest existing institutional analogue to the thesis's X4 proposal. Its rationale is allocation of responsibility and avoidance of misunderstanding, not effort reduction; no effect data were found.

proposition_tested: P1.6 / P1.1 (comfort procedures exist partly to build the recipient's defense record).
observed_finding: AS 6101.02 states that because of §11, underwriters 'request accountants to assist them in developing a record of reasonable investigation' and that a comfort letter is 'one of a number of procedures' that may be used to establish a reasonable investigation. Para .43 states that where requirements for negative assurance are not met, accountants 'are limited to reporting procedures performed and findings obtained'.
population_and_setting: As above
outcome_measured: Purpose and permitted forms of comfort
short_exact_excerpt: Consequently, underwriters request accountants to assist them in developing a record of reasonable investigation.
limitations: Statement of purpose by the standard-setter; not evidence on actual use.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: third-party diligence outputs in project finance also serve as part of the lender's documented process (credit file), which is a reason recipients demand them even when they add little new information. Verify: credit-policy requirements for consultant reports as file documents.
analyst_inference: Supports a 'record-building' function of outside work for the recipient: part of the demand for advisor output is to document the recipient's own diligence, which neither eliminates the recipient's work nor is fully captured by detection metrics.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (does disclosure of procedures performed and findings — without an assurance conclusion — satisfy recipients?).
observed_finding: Under current AS 6101, after the 135-day window the comfort letter is limited to 'procedures performed and findings obtained' ('management inquiries'), and Davis Polk states that investment banks are usually unwilling to proceed with an offering without a customary negative assurance paragraph. It reports that the gap between Q3 period end and the 10-K deadline can be up to 182 days, creating up to a 47-day window in which an issuer is effectively precluded from offering; the PCAOB proposal (Nov. 2026) would tie the outside date to filing deadlines and add a note that auditors are not required to give negative assurance and listing factors for that decision.
population_and_setting: US underwriters and issuers in SEC-registered offerings (incl. foreign private issuers, proposed semiannual filers)
study_or_observation_method: Law-firm client update describing proposal and market practice
intervention_and_comparator: Comfort letter with negative assurance vs letter limited to procedures and findings
outcome_measured: Underwriters' willingness to proceed with an offering
quantitative_result: Per Davis Polk: Q3-end-to-10-K gap up to 182 days -> up to 47-day window without negative assurance; up to 212 days for proposed small non-accelerated filers; up to 274 days for semiannual filers. No counts of deals delayed or abandoned.
short_exact_excerpt: investment banks are usually unwilling to proceed with an offering if the comfort letter does not include a customary negative assurance paragraph
limitations: Practitioner assertion without data; firm has a stated policy position. Underlying PCAOB release not reviewed directly (pcaobus.org docket blocked scripted access).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers as counterevidence to CL026: sophisticated recipients treat a disclosure of procedures performed and findings as NOT equivalent to a producer's (even limited) conclusion — they want the expert to commit to 'nothing came to our attention'. In renewable-energy credit, a consultant report that lists checks without an opinion may likewise fail to satisfy credit committees. Verify: whether lenders accept 'findings-only' consultant reports or require opinions/negative assurance.
analyst_inference: Challenges the assumption that coverage visibility alone substitutes for producer judgment. Recipients appear to demand a producer conclusion with accountability attached (here, negative assurance) — likely because it supports their legal defense and shifts some responsibility — so 'procedures and findings, including none' is a complement, not a replacement. Stated-practice evidence, not observed behavior counts.

proposition_tested: P2.4 (findings without assurance: the user, not the producer, must judge appropriateness and draw conclusions).
observed_finding: For AUP engagements the IAASB introduced acceptance conditions that the engaging party 'acknowledges that the expected procedures ... are appropriate for the purpose' and that procedures and findings can be described objectively 'not subject to varying interpretations'; it required the engagement letter and report to explain that findings are 'the factual results' of the procedures; and it replaced the report statement that the engagement 'does not constitute a reasonable or limited assurance engagement' with 'is not an assurance engagement' because respondents were concerned the phrase 'may not be well understood by intended users'. An AUP engagement 'does not involve obtaining evidence for the purpose of the practitioner expressing an opinion or an assurance conclusion in any form.'
population_and_setting: Practitioners performing agreed-upon procedures on financial or non-financial subject matter (international)
