study_or_observation_method: Standard-setter's basis for conclusions summarizing exposure-draft responses
outcome_measured: Report/engagement design requirements
short_exact_excerpt: The engaging party acknowledges that the expected procedures to be performed by the practitioner are appropriate for the purpose of the AUP engagement;
limitations: Basis for conclusions, not the standard text; user-misunderstanding concern is respondents' view, not measured.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: a 'procedures performed and findings (incl. none)' diligence product resembles an AUP report: it shifts the judgment of whether the checks suffice, and what the findings mean, onto the recipient. For renewable-energy diligence, an advisor offering checks-and-findings outputs would leave interpretation and sufficiency with the investment/credit team. Verify: whether recipients of such outputs spend less time than with opinion-style reports, or more (because they must draw the conclusions).
analyst_inference: Clarifies what CL026-style disclosure does and does not do: it makes coverage visible (X4) but expressly transfers sufficiency and interpretation to the user (W1). The standard-setter itself worried users misread assurance terminology — suggesting coverage disclosure can be misunderstood as assurance (a P2.3-type risk).

proposition_tested: P1.1 (conditions under which decision-makers may rely on an outside expert without independent investigation).
observed_finding: The court held the board was presumed to have relied in good faith on its compensation consultant (Graef Crystal) under §141(e) and that plaintiffs must plead particularized facts showing, e.g., (a) no actual reliance; (b) reliance not in good faith; (c) directors did not reasonably believe the advice was within the expert's competence; (d) the expert was not selected with reasonable care, attributable to the directors; (e) the material, reasonably available subject matter was 'so obvious' that failing to consider it was grossly negligent regardless of the expert's advice; or (f) waste/fraud. Due care is 'process due care only'.
population_and_setting: Disney shareholders v. directors (Ovitz employment/severance); Delaware Supreme Court, derivative suit
intervention_and_comparator: Reliance on outside expert vs uninformed decision
outcome_measured: Conditions for §141(e) protection
source_locator: 746 A.2d 244, section 'Plaintiffs’ Contention that the Old Board Violated the Process Duty of Care in Approving the Ovitz Employment Agreement'
short_exact_excerpt: (e) the subject matter (in this case the cost calculation) that was material and reasonably available was so obvious that the board’s failure to consider it was grossly negligent regardless of the expert’s advice or lack of advice
limitations: Pleading-stage list ('for example'); gross-negligence standard is more forgiving than §11's negligence-type standard; Delaware-specific.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers to investment committees relying on outside advisors (e.g., fairness or valuation advisors for project acquisitions, market price-curve consultants): reliance is protected when the advisor was chosen with care, acted within expertise, and nothing material was obviously missing. Difference: lenders' regulators (SR 26-2, TPRM — already in register) impose their own oversight expectations. Verify: IC charters' language on reliance on advisors.
analyst_inference: Defines the boundary for decision-makers in terms of selection, competence, good faith and an 'obviousness' exception — none of which requires re-performing the expert's work. The 'obvious material gap' exception means the recipient must still scan for glaring omissions (W1), which is where explicit coverage/omission statements (X4) could matter.

proposition_tested: P1.3 (advisor omissions) — does an expert's incomplete work make the recipient's reliance improper?
observed_finding: Although the total severance cost was material and 'reasonably available' (the expert or board could have calculated it) and the expert later said 'nobody' quantified it, the court held the expert's hindsight regret did not rebut the presumption of proper reliance; the board must consider 'only material facts that are reasonably available', not every fact; the expert was the board's adviser ex ante, 'not their agent ex post to make binding admissions'. The court left open that a properly pleaded complaint could rebut reliance.
population_and_setting: As above
intervention_and_comparator: Expert's omitted calculation
outcome_measured: Whether omission defeats directors' reliance
source_locator: 746 A.2d 244, sections 'Analytical Framework for the Informational Component of Directorial Decisionmaking' and process-duty-of-care section
short_exact_excerpt: The Board is responsible for considering only material facts that are reasonably available, not those that are immaterial or out of the Board’s reasonable reach.
limitations: Later trial (In re Walt Disney, 2005/2006) not reviewed here; pleading-stage holding only.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: if a consultant omits an analysis (e.g., downside curtailment scenario), the recipient's reliance may still be proper unless the gap was obvious and material. Making omissions explicit (X4) would make gaps 'obvious' and arguably shift them into the recipient's W1 scope. Verify: whether IC memos record advisor scope exclusions.
analyst_inference: Under Delaware's standard, advisor omissions (W3 risk) do not automatically convert into recipient fault; but transparency about omissions could make them obvious and so expand what the recipient must address — a possible tension with the thesis's effort-reduction claim (inference).

proposition_tested: P1.1 / P2.4 (reliance requires a substantive report with a knowable basis; uninformed reliance is unprotected).
observed_finding: Directors approved a merger after a 20-minute oral presentation with no documents; the court held the CEO's oral presentation and the CFO's statement did not qualify as §141(e) 'reports' (the former 'lacked substance' because the presenter was uninformed of key terms). Directors were entitled to rely on the chairman's opinion of value 'provided that such opinion was reached on a sound basis', but had they informed themselves they would have learned 'the source and derivation of the $55 price and could not reasonably have relied thereupon in good faith'. The court stated an outside valuation or fairness opinion is not required as a matter of law and insiders may be better placed.
population_and_setting: Trans Union shareholders v. directors (cash-out merger); Delaware Supreme Court
outcome_measured: Whether directors were informed / entitled to §141(e) protection
quantitative_result: Board deliberation based on a '20-minute oral presentation' (court's description); no written summary or valuation documents before the board.
source_locator: 488 A.2d 858, discussion of the September 20 meeting and §141(e) (text and footnotes)
short_exact_excerpt: Under § 141(e), the directors were entitled to rely upon their chairman’s opinion of value and adequacy, provided that such opinion was reached on a sound basis.
limitations: Concerns reliance on insiders, not outside experts; heavily criticized and followed by statutory exculpation (§102(b)(7)).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Transfers: an IC that adopts an advisor's valuation without knowing how it was derived risks unprotected reliance; legitimate reliance requires access to the basis (assumptions, derivation). Traceable assumptions (X3/X4) are therefore not only a convenience but bear on whether reliance is defensible. Verify: whether IC approvals record the derivation of key numbers (e.g., price curves, P50/P90).
analyst_inference: Supports the thesis that visibility into the basis of an opinion matters for legitimate reliance: the reliance failure was precisely that the derivation was unknown. It does not show that such visibility reduces effort — the duty is to be informed, which may require more reading.

proposition_tested: P1.3 / P1.2 / P1.1 (why recipients duplicate an outside party's diligence).
observed_finding: Clifford Chance reports that borrower/vendor-produced due diligence reports for lenders and purchasers are 'rarely popular' and that 'certain institutional financing bodies will typically insist on engaging their own counsel'; it says it is 'increasingly coming across' vendor diligence 'below basic standards' that 'causes far more trouble (and thus time and cost) than it saves'; reports that 'simply recite or reword' underlying documents leave recipient counsel effectively reading the documents; recommends evaluative content, agreeing report style with beneficiaries in advance, and warns that restricted document access undermines precedent (a contractor's claimed 'banked' liability cap had never been seen by lenders' counsel).
population_and_setting: Project/construction financings and asset sales (energy and infrastructure sectors implied); lenders, purchasers and their counsel
study_or_observation_method: Practitioner blog drawing on firm experience
outcome_measured: Recipient acceptance and re-work of vendor/borrower diligence
short_exact_excerpt: We have seen too many reports lately that simply recite or reword at length the drafting from the underlying documents - in which case the purchaser/lender counsel might as well be reading the actual documents.
limitations: Anecdotal; author's firm has an interest in lenders engaging their own counsel; no frequency or effort data.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Directly in-domain for renewable-energy project finance: duplicate legal diligence by lenders' counsel arises from (i) institutional policy requiring own counsel (W1/W4), (ii) descriptive rather than evaluative reports (W2/W3), and (iii) restricted access to source documents (X3). Verify: share of deals where lenders accept vendor DD with reliance vs commission their own.
analyst_inference: Separates causes of duplicate work: some is policy-mandated and would persist (W1/W4), some is caused by low-value outputs and lack of access (W2/W3). The latter is the part a traceable, evaluative product could plausibly address.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (reliance is allocated contractually; non-reliance recipients receive information without the legal ability to rely).
observed_finding: EAIF's RfP for a Lenders' Technical Advisor on a Kenyan biogas project states the LTA's report 'will be prepared primarily for the Lenders but may be shared with the equity and mezzanine investors on a non-reliance basis'; scope includes a conceptual-phase feasibility analysis 'including red flags', detailed design review and construction/commissioning monitoring.
population_and_setting: Development-finance lender procuring technical due diligence for a renewable (biogas) project, 2021
outcome_measured: Reliance allocation and scope of LTA work
short_exact_excerpt: The LTA’s report will be prepared primarily for the Lenders but may be shared with the equity and mezzanine investors on a non-reliance basis.
limitations: Single RfP; intended allocation only; does not show what equity investors did with the report.
transferability_to_target_workflow: In-domain: in renewable-energy financings the same technical report may circulate to parties with and without reliance rights; the non-reliance parties must decide for themselves whether to commission or perform their own review. Verify: whether equity/mezzanine investors in such deals commission separate technical advisors.
analyst_inference: Who may rely is set by contract, not by the report's quality; identical transparency can carry different implications for recipients' required work depending on reliance rights. This adds a contractual boundary alongside the statutory (§11) and fiduciary (§141(e)) ones.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Integrating outside evidence into the recipient's system reduces duplicated work end-to-end
observed_finding: Across 17 articles (42 studies) on PACS, regional image exchange, interoperable EHRs, CD import tools and HIE, image sharing technology was associated with a significant decrease in repeat imaging; the decrease was larger in the most rigorous studies.
evidence_type: systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (mostly observational primary studies)
population_and_setting: Published and grey English-language literature 2004-2014; 58.8% of articles set in emergency departments; mostly U.S.
study_or_observation_method: Random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression of standardized effect sizes; risk-of-bias rating on 7 safeguards
intervention_and_comparator: Image sharing technology available vs not available (or before vs after)
outcome_measured: Repeat (including unnecessary) imaging utilization
quantitative_result: Repeat imaging pooled ES = -0.17 (95% CI -0.25 to -0.09; P < .001). Most rigorous studies (n = 25 studies with >=4 safeguards): repeat imaging ES = -0.27 (95% CI -0.33 to -0.21). Heterogeneity I^2 = 98%. 57% of all studies found some reduction.
source_locator: Abstract (Results); Results section 'Estimated Effect of Image Sharing Technology on Imaging Utilization'; Appendix 1 secondary analysis
short_exact_excerpt: Image sharing technology was associated with a significant decrease in repeat imaging (pooled effect size [ES] = -0.17; 95% confidence interval [CI] = [-0.25, -0.09]; P < .001).
limitations: Standardized effect size not converted into natural units; most studies at moderate/high risk of bias; overlaps with primary studies in other reviews and with Lu 2012 (register SRC123); outcome is test utilization, not clinician effort.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: evidence already produced elsewhere is less likely to be regenerated when it is available inside the recipient's own system at the point of decision. Differences: a repeat scan is a discrete, countable duplicate with a clear definition; IC 'reconstruction' (re-running energy yield, re-checking interconnection or offtake assumptions) is analytic work, partly mandated (W1), with no standard duplicate definition. Needs verification: whether IC teams re-derive advisor numbers because the evidence is not in their model/data room (W2/W5) versus because policy requires independent derivation (W1).
analyst_inference: Integration of outside evidence reliably reduces duplicate regeneration of that same evidence, but the authors themselves call the effect 'modest'; this replicates the direction of Lu 2012 at scale, not its magnitude (Lu's 72%->11% is a single-site extreme).

proposition_tested: P3.2 Integration shifts effort/utilization elsewhere rather than removing it (offset)
observed_finding: The same technologies were associated with a significant increase in any imaging utilization, and for all outcomes combined image sharing was not associated with utilization. Authors suggest easier access may also make ordering easier, particularly in EHRs.
population_and_setting: As R3D-E01
intervention_and_comparator: Image sharing technology vs none
outcome_measured: Any imaging utilization; all utilization outcomes combined
quantitative_result: Any imaging pooled ES = 0.20 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.32; P = .002); most rigorous studies 0.17 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.30). All outcomes combined ES = 0.00 (95% CI -0.07 to 0.07; P = .991). Meta-regression repeat vs any imaging beta = -0.58 (95% CI -0.84 to -0.33).
short_exact_excerpt: However, image sharing technology was associated with a significant increase in any imaging utilization (pooled ES = 0.20; 95% CI = [0.07, 0.32]; P = .002).
limitations: 'Any imaging' and 'repeat imaging' come largely from different studies, so the offset is not observed within the same populations; mechanism for the increase is the authors' conjecture.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: making more outside analysis easily available inside the recipient's system may expand the volume of analysis requested/consumed (more scenarios, more checks) even while removing duplication. Needs verification in IC settings: whether integrated advisor outputs reduce total diligence hours or just reallocate them.
analyst_inference: This is the clearest quantitative sign that 'duplicate avoided' and 'total work reduced' are different outcomes; a vendor claiming reduced reconstruction should be asked for total-effort, not just duplicate-rate, metrics.

proposition_tested: P3.1 / P3.2 — whether review effort added by integration has been measured
observed_finding: The review states it does not assess efficiency, satisfaction or cost; generalizability is limited because many studies used one organization or one technology; effects could not be stratified by modality, patient or condition.
population_and_setting: As R3D-E01
outcome_measured: Scope of outcomes covered by the literature
limitations: Statement about this review's scope, not proof that no efficiency studies exist.
transferability_to_target_workflow: The imaging literature measures avoided duplicate production (scans), not the reviewing clinician's time to locate, open and interpret outside material — the quantity most analogous to IC-team review effort. Transfer to 'review time saved' is therefore an inference, not an observation.
analyst_inference: Absence of evidence on review time: the medical analog cannot tell us whether integration adds reading/reconciliation work for the receiving professional.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Integrating outside records reduces duplicated testing
observed_finding: Of 34 HIE outcome studies, low-quality evidence generally finds HIE reduces duplicative laboratory and radiology testing. Laboratory testing: 4 ED studies reported reduced testing; of 2 ambulatory studies, one found increased testing and one a slowing of growth. Radiology: 7 ED studies reported reduced testing; of 2 ambulatory studies one reported a decrease and one no change.
population_and_setting: Studies of HIE in clinical or public health settings, any country, 1990-Feb 2015
study_or_observation_method: Systematic review with dual extraction; strength of evidence rated
intervention_and_comparator: HIE availability/use vs none
outcome_measured: Duplicative laboratory and radiology testing, ED costs, admissions
quantitative_result: 34 studies included (2 RCTs, 32 observational/survey). Lab testing: 6 studies (4 ED reductions; ambulatory: 1 increase, 1 slowed growth). Radiology: 9 studies (7 ED reductions; ambulatory: 1 decrease, 1 no change). Strength of evidence: low.
source_locator: Abstract (Results); Results, 'Improving Resource Use' and Table 2
short_exact_excerpt: Low-quality evidence generally finds that HIE reduces duplicative laboratory and radiology testing, emergency department costs, hospital admissions (less so for readmissions)
limitations: Counts of studies, not pooled effects; retrospective designs; heterogeneous HIE types.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Effects concentrate in high-tempo ED settings where the alternative to using outside evidence is fast regeneration; ambulatory (slower, more deliberative) settings are mixed — closer to the deliberative IC setting. Mechanism that transfers: evidence already produced elsewhere is less likely to be regenerated when it is available inside the recipient's own system at the point of decision. Differences: a repeat scan is a discrete, countable duplicate with a clear definition; IC 'reconstruction' (re-running energy yield, re-checking interconnection or offtake assumptions) is analytic work, partly mandated (W1), with no standard duplicate definition. Needs verification: whether IC teams re-derive advisor numbers because the evidence is not in their model/data room (W2/W5) versus because policy requires independent derivation (W1).
analyst_inference: Setting moderates: the duplicate-avoidance benefit is strongest where regeneration is quick and the outside evidence is immediately decision-relevant; deliberative settings show mixed results.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Integrating outside records reduces duplicated procedures (rigorous designs)
observed_finding: 24 articles (63 analyses, 2014-2017): 7 studies with designs suitable for causal inference all reported some beneficial effect, none adverse; benefits include fewer duplicated procedures and reduced imaging. Community HIEs were more likely to report benefits than enterprise or vendor-mediated exchange.
population_and_setting: Mostly U.S. studies from 9 states; ~40% of analyses from a handful of New York HIEs
study_or_observation_method: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed and Scopus; classification of analyses as beneficial/null/adverse
intervention_and_comparator: HIE vs no HIE
outcome_measured: Utilization, cost, quality, safety outcomes
quantitative_result: All 63 analyses: 68.3% beneficial, 7.9% adverse, remainder no effect. Rigorous designs: 7 of 24 articles (13 of 63 analyses); 10 of 13 analyses beneficial, 3 no effect, 0 adverse. Study level: community HIEs 70.3% vs other types 54.2% reporting benefit (P = .04). One study (Eftekhari et al.) found reduced repetition of therapeutic but not diagnostic procedures; one Israeli cohort found HIE adversely related to number of imaging tests ordered.
source_locator: Abstract; Results — 'Rigorous Studies', 'Healthcare Utilization', 'HIE Type'; Tables 1 and 3
short_exact_excerpt: Seven of the 24 studies used designs suitable for causal inference and all reported some beneficial effect from HIE; none reported adverse effects.
limitations: Vote counting hides magnitudes; New York concentration; publication bias possible; percentages and derived counts partly from automated extraction of full text.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests shared, neutral, multi-party infrastructure (community HIE) outperforms enterprise/vendor-specific exchange — analogous to a common evidence format usable across advisors and investors vs bespoke supplier portals. Mechanism that transfers: evidence already produced elsewhere is less likely to be regenerated when it is available inside the recipient's own system at the point of decision. Differences: a repeat scan is a discrete, countable duplicate with a clear definition; IC 'reconstruction' (re-running energy yield, re-checking interconnection or offtake assumptions) is analytic work, partly mandated (W1), with no standard duplicate definition. Needs verification: whether IC teams re-derive advisor numbers because the evidence is not in their model/data room (W2/W5) versus because policy requires independent derivation (W1).
analyst_inference: Better-designed studies point the same way as weaker ones, which strengthens the direction of effect; but 'some beneficial effect' is not 'large effect', and adverse/null analyses (~32%) persist.

proposition_tested: P3.1 qualified: availability of outside evidence vs actual use in workflow
observed_finding: Low-quality evidence from 12 hypothesis-testing studies supports reduced ED use or costs; direct evidence from 21 studies (13 HIE organizations) generally showed provider usage in less than 10% of patient encounters; barriers include technical and workflow issues, costs and privacy.
population_and_setting: English-language quantitative studies of exchange among unaffiliated organizations, 2003-May 2014
intervention_and_comparator: HIE availability/use
outcome_measured: HIE usage rates; ED utilization/costs; barriers
quantitative_result: 12 hypothesis-testing studies (ED use/costs, low-quality); 21 usage studies from 13 HIE organizations (6 in New York): usage generally <10% of patient encounters; ~one quarter of HIE organizations financially stable (17 studies).
short_exact_excerpt: Direct evidence that HIEs were used by providers was reported in 21 studies involving 13 distinct HIE organizations, 6 of which were located in New York, and generally showed usage in less than 10% of patient encounters.
limitations: Abstract only; usage figures may be outdated (pre-2014) and vary by organization.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: an outside-evidence channel that sits outside the recipient's working tools is rarely opened, so its duplicate-avoidance potential is unrealized. For IC workflows: a separate advisor portal may see low use unless evidence lands inside the model, memo or data room the team already works in. Needs verification: actual usage logs of advisor deliverables by IC teams.
analyst_inference: Low usage is a strong reason why 'integration into the recipient's own system' (Lu: imported to PACS; Sodickson: CD import) differs from mere 'access' — and why population-level effects are smaller than single-site import effects.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Integrating outside evidence reduces duplicated work at scale (multi-site)
observed_finding: Comparing 37 EDs that initiated HIE participation with 410 that did not (California and Florida, 2007-2010), HIE was associated with reduced probability of repeat imaging at unaffiliated EDs within 30 days for CT, ultrasound and chest x-ray.
evidence_type: observational panel (difference-in-differences style with ED fixed effects and trends)
population_and_setting: ED discharge data, State Emergency Department Databases, CA and FL, 2007-2010; 447 EDs
study_or_observation_method: Regression with ED fixed effects and trends; HIE participation from HIMSS data
intervention_and_comparator: EDs initiating HIE participation (n=37) vs non-participating EDs (n=410)
outcome_measured: Probability of repeat CT, ultrasound, chest x-ray (same study, same body region, within 30 days at unaffiliated ED)
quantitative_result: Baseline repeat rates: CT 14.7% (20,139 repeats), ultrasound 20.7% (13,060), chest x-ray 19.5% (29,703). HIE effect: CT -8.7 percentage points (95% CI -14.7 to -2.7); ultrasound -9.1 pp (95% CI -17.2 to -1.1); chest x-ray -13.0 pp (95% CI -18.3 to -7.7); 44%-67% relative to sample means.
short_exact_excerpt: HIE was associated with reduced probability of repeat ED imaging in all 3 modalities
limitations: Abstract only; exposure is hospital participation not clinician use; wide CIs; early-adopter EDs may differ; only repeats across unaffiliated EDs counted.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: evidence already produced elsewhere is less likely to be regenerated when it is available inside the recipient's own system at the point of decision. Differences: a repeat scan is a discrete, countable duplicate with a clear definition; IC 'reconstruction' (re-running energy yield, re-checking interconnection or offtake assumptions) is analytic work, partly mandated (W1), with no standard duplicate definition. Needs verification: whether IC teams re-derive advisor numbers because the evidence is not in their model/data room (W2/W5) versus because policy requires independent derivation (W1).
analyst_inference: A multi-site estimate with relative reductions (44-67%) comparable to single-site studies — the strongest pro-integration evidence found; however, it contrasts with the national 2018 null in R3D-E10, suggesting context or period dependence.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Importing outside evidence into the recipient's own system reduces duplicated work (replication of Lu 2012 at another site)
observed_finding: Among ED transfer patients, successful import of outside-hospital CDs into the receiving PACS was followed by fewer subsequent diagnostic exams and CTs within 24 hours than failed import, and fewer CTs than a pre-implementation historical control.
evidence_type: retrospective cohort (successful vs failed import) plus historical control
population_and_setting: 1,487 consecutive ED transfer patients with outside CDs, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Feb-Aug 2009; historical control 254 patients Aug 2007-Jan 2008
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of imaging counts within 24h after import attempt; Wilcoxon rank sum tests
intervention_and_comparator: Successful CD import to PACS (78%, 1161/1487) vs failed import; and vs historical controls before import procedures
outcome_measured: Mean diagnostic exams and CT scans per patient within 24 hours
quantitative_result: All diagnostic imaging: 3.30 (failed) vs 2.74 (successful) exams/patient, 17% reduction (P < .001). CT: 1.41 vs 1.19 scans/patient, 16% reduction (P = .01). Versus historical control: CT 1.18 vs 0.84 scans/patient, 29% reduction (P < .001). Import failure rate 22%.
short_exact_excerpt: CD import of outside imaging from the sending institution into the receiving institution's PACS significantly decreased the rates of subsequent imaging utilization.
limitations: Single site; non-random import failure; abstract only; import itself requires staff processing (not quantified in abstract).
transferability_to_target_workflow: Most direct analog to 'integrating advisor outputs into the client's own system': the same outside evidence, once in the native system, is regenerated less. Mechanism that transfers: evidence already produced elsewhere is less likely to be regenerated when it is available inside the recipient's own system at the point of decision. Differences: a repeat scan is a discrete, countable duplicate with a clear definition; IC 'reconstruction' (re-running energy yield, re-checking interconnection or offtake assumptions) is analytic work, partly mandated (W1), with no standard duplicate definition. Needs verification: whether IC teams re-derive advisor numbers because the evidence is not in their model/data room (W2/W5) versus because policy requires independent derivation (W1).
analyst_inference: Replicates Lu 2012's direction at a second academic center but with a smaller effect (16-29% vs Lu's 52%->11% CD vs imported contrast), consistent with Lu being an upper-bound estimate.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Integrated outside records reduce duplicated tests; P3.2 the integration work is relocated to new staff
observed_finding: In one ED, patients whose care included an HIE query had fewer lab tests and radiology exams than controls; the queries were performed by medical liaisons hired to query the HIE and provide the history to ED clinicians.
population_and_setting: One suburban ED, Western New York (HEALTHeLINK HIE), March 27 - May 24, 2014; 698 treatment and 1,275 control patients
study_or_observation_method: Negative binomial regression of test counts; controls were patients treated during shifts without liaisons
intervention_and_comparator: HIE query by dedicated liaison for every encounter vs no HIE query
outcome_measured: Number of laboratory tests and radiology examinations per patient
quantitative_result: Laboratory tests: coefficient -0.72 (SE 0.13, p<.01), ~52% reduction in expected count. Radiology exams: coefficient -0.44 (SE 0.07, p<.01), ~36% reduction. No CIs reported.
short_exact_excerpt: A group of medical liaisons were hired to query the medical history of patients from an HIE and provide it to the ED clinicians.
limitations: Non-random shift assignment; 2 months; one ED; effect is of a staffed intermediary service; no measure of clinician reading time. Liaison staffing cost/time not netted against savings in the analysis reviewed.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: the duplicate-avoidance benefit appeared when someone else did the retrieval/integration labor and delivered evidence to the decision-maker — analogous to an advisor or analyst pre-integrating evidence into the IC memo. Difference: the cost of that intermediary labor was not netted against savings, so end-to-end effort reduction is unknown.
analyst_inference: Large effect, but it shows integration labor relocated to a dedicated role rather than eliminated; supports P3.1 for duplicated production and P3.2 for where the work went.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Integration reduces duplicated work at scale (national test)
observed_finding: In 2018 national Medicare data, fragmented readmissions (to a different hospital) had higher odds of repeat same-body-system imaging, and this was not mitigated when both hospitals shared an HIE; the authors conclude HIEs as deployed are not associated with decreased repeat imaging in readmissions.
population_and_setting: 275,860 admission-readmission pairs (269,348 patients, 3,436 hospitals), Medicare FFS 2018; 13.2% of pairs with Alzheimer disease
study_or_observation_method: Unadjusted and adjusted logistic regression with readmission-hospital fixed effects; HIE exposure from AHA IT Supplement
intervention_and_comparator: Fragmented readmission to hospital sharing same HIE (4.6% of pairs) vs non-fragmented same-hospital readmission (66.0%); also different-HIE, no-HIE, missing
outcome_measured: Repeat imaging of same body system during 30-day readmission
quantitative_result: 14.3% of beneficiaries had repeat imaging. Fragmented vs non-fragmented: ~5% higher odds (no AD). Same-HIE fragmented readmissions: AOR 1.06 (95% CI 1.00-1.13). No difference for beneficiaries with AD.
source_locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusions), p. 66; Results p. 67-68; Conclusions p. 69-70
short_exact_excerpt: Despite substantial investment, HIEs as currently deployed and used are not associated with decreased odds of repeat imaging in readmissions.
limitations: Exposure is hospital-reported participation, not use; 16.3% missing HIE data; unknown whether images or only reports shared; inpatient readmission setting differs from ED studies.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism that transfers: institutional membership in an evidence-sharing network does not by itself change recipients' regeneration behavior. For IC workflows: subscribing to/receiving a structured advisor product is not the same as integrating it into the team's working model and memo. Mechanism that transfers: evidence already produced elsewhere is less likely to be regenerated when it is available inside the recipient's own system at the point of decision. Differences: a repeat scan is a discrete, countable duplicate with a clear definition; IC 'reconstruction' (re-running energy yield, re-checking interconnection or offtake assumptions) is analytic work, partly mandated (W1), with no standard duplicate definition. Needs verification: whether IC teams re-derive advisor numbers because the evidence is not in their model/data room (W2/W5) versus because policy requires independent derivation (W1).
analyst_inference: The strongest counterevidence found: at national scale and in a later period, 'integration' measured as network presence shows no reduction. Reconciles with E06/E08 if the active ingredient is point-of-care integration, not connectivity.

proposition_tested: P1.6 / P3.2 Recipients regenerate evidence despite access because of search cost, missing content, or distrust of outside interpretation
observed_finding: Authors offer (as possibilities, not tested) that it may be easier to order a test than search an HIE, that needed information may not be in the HIE, that HIE presence is not HIE use, and that a repeat test may be ordered because the provider does not trust another hospital's interpretation; they also note not all repeat imaging is wasteful.
population_and_setting: As R3D-E10
study_or_observation_method: Discussion section reasoning, citing prior survey work on reasons for low HIE use
source_locator: Discussion p. 69 ('Possible reasons for this association...'); Conclusions p. 70
short_exact_excerpt: Possible reasons for this association could include that it is easier to order a test instead of searching through an HIE for past results
limitations: Untested hypotheses; no data on clinician reasoning in this study.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Maps directly onto IC reconstruction drivers: search cost (W2/W5), incompleteness of outside evidence (W3), distrust of outside interpretation (P1.6), and legitimate re-analysis (W1). Needs verification by observing why IC analysts re-run advisor analyses.
analyst_inference: Even in medicine, duplicate avoidance depends on whether the outside evidence is complete and trusted, not merely present — consistent with RQ1 findings that review persists for reasons beyond access.

proposition_tested: P3.1 Electronic integration of third-party data into credit decisions reduces end-to-end processing time without loss of quality
observed_finding: FinTech mortgage lenders (online applications, electronic collection and automated verification of borrower data against third-party databases, centralized partially automated underwriting) process applications faster than other lenders, with lower FHA default rates and no significant difference in interest rates.
evidence_type: observational loan-level comparison with fixed effects (analog)
population_and_setting: Near-universe of U.S. mortgage applications/originations 2010-2016 (HMDA and other loan-level data)
study_or_observation_method: OLS of processing days on FinTech-lender indicator with loan/borrower controls and census tract-month fixed effects; FHA default regressions
intervention_and_comparator: FinTech lenders vs other lenders (banks and non-banks)
outcome_measured: Days from application to closing; ex-post default (FHA loans); interest rates
quantitative_result: About 10 days faster, ~20% of average processing time; purchase loans 7.9 days (15% of 52-day mean) to ~18% with controls/FE; refinances 9.3-14.6 days faster (17%-29% of 51-day mean). FHA default rates on FinTech mortgages about 25% lower than traditional lenders with loan controls; no significant interest-rate difference.
source_locator: Abstract; Introduction pp. 1-2; Section 'A. Processing time results' (Table 3) p. 12
short_exact_excerpt: we find that FinTech lenders reduce processing time by about 10 days, or 20% of the average processing time.
limitations: Lender-type comparison bundles many features; selection of borrowers partly addressed but not eliminated; mortgage underwriting is highly standardized; WP version.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: when third-party evidence arrives electronically and is checked automatically inside the lender's own system, end-to-end cycle time falls without measured quality loss. Differences: renewable project finance diligence is bespoke, low-volume, judgment-heavy, and relies on advisor reports (IE, energy yield, legal) rather than databases; quality outcome (project default) is rare and slow.
analyst_inference: A credible end-to-end (not task-level) finance analog showing moderate (~20%) cycle-time gains — much smaller than task-level automation claims — with quality preserved. It does not isolate reviewer effort.

proposition_tested: P3.3 / P5.1 Standardized, automatable steps shrink while non-automated steps and human underwriting remain
observed_finding: Authors state automation does not eliminate human underwriters but makes processing less labor-intensive and more standardized and repeatable; the larger refinance advantage may reflect that purchase loans always require a locally administered, not-yet-automated appraisal.
population_and_setting: As R3D-E12
study_or_observation_method: Institutional background (industry interviews) and interpretation of heterogeneous effects
intervention_and_comparator: FinTech vs other lenders; refinance vs purchase
outcome_measured: Processing time by loan type
quantitative_result: Refinance advantage 9.3-14.6 days vs purchase 7.9 days (see R3D-E12).
source_locator: Section on FinTech business model pp. 6-7; Section 'A. Processing time results' p. 12
short_exact_excerpt: This approach does not eliminate the role of human underwriters, but does make mortgage processing less labor-intensive.
limitations: Appraisal explanation is the authors' interpretation; human underwriting time not measured.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Analog for IC workflows: the end-to-end gain is bounded by the slowest non-integrated, judgment- or site-specific step (here appraisal; in renewables e.g. IE site review, interconnection studies, legal title work).
analyst_inference: End-to-end gains are capped by residual human/bespoke steps — consistent with P3.3 that drafting/assembly is the most reducible portion.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: Integrating analysis developed by someone else reduces the recipient's follow-up work partly by reducing skeptical action on red flags (lower scrutiny, not just less duplication)
observed_finding: In an experiment with 173 audit practitioners in which a data analytic test flagged a potential fraud red flag, auditors who inherited the test (developed by someone else) were less likely to take skeptical actions than auditors who developed it; mediation analyses point to reduced psychological ownership.
population_and_setting: 173 audit practitioners (rank/experience not verified)
study_or_observation_method: Three-condition experiment: developed ADA; inherited ADA; inherited ADA plus development memo
intervention_and_comparator: Inherited (outside-developed) ADA vs self-developed ADA
outcome_measured: Whether participants judged more work was needed and escalated (skeptical action); sales estimates
quantitative_result: Per university press release: 54% (developed) vs 26% (inherited) said more work was needed and escalated. Cell sizes and test statistics not verified.
source_locator: Abstract (VU research portal excerpt); NC State press release 2025-09 (percentages)
short_exact_excerpt: auditors who inherited the ADA are less likely to exercise skeptical actions
limitations: Full text blocked (403); percentages from press release; hypothetical setting; single red flag; one analytic type.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Directly relevant to IC teams receiving an advisor's model or analysis: less follow-up on an inherited analysis may look like 'reduced reconstruction' but can be reduced scrutiny of genuine red flags. Needs verification: whether IC reviewers of advisor-built models follow up on anomalies less than on in-house models.
analyst_inference: Key caution for RQ3: lower recipient work after integration is not automatically a benefit — part of it may be lost skepticism (P2.3-like effect on reliance). Effort reduction must be measured jointly with error/red-flag detection.

proposition_tested: P2.4 Visibility into how the analysis was developed (scope, process) improves appropriate reliance
observed_finding: Providing inheriting auditors with a brief memorandum documenting the test's development mitigated the negative effect of inheriting on skeptical actions, partially (not fully) closing the gap.
population_and_setting: As R3D-E14
intervention_and_comparator: Inherited ADA + development memo vs inherited ADA alone (and vs developed)
outcome_measured: Skeptical action rate
quantitative_result: Per press release: 34% (inherited + memo) vs 26% (inherited) vs 54% (developed). Statistical significance not verified.
source_locator: Abstract (search excerpt); NC State press release
short_exact_excerpt: a brief memorandum documenting the ADA's development
limitations: As R3D-E14; memo effect size is modest and partial.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Suggests that advisor deliverables documenting how analyses were built (assumptions, data, checks performed) can partly restore recipients' appropriate scrutiny — but only partly. Needs verification in investment settings.
analyst_inference: Provenance/process documentation improves appropriate follow-up, not just trust — modest support for X3/X4-type features, with the caveat that the effect is partial.

proposition_tested: P3.1 qualified / P3.2: task-level automation gains shrink end-to-end; analyst validation remains
observed_finding: Vendor reports that its automated financial spreading tool gave a top global bank's wholesale credit team a 70% acceleration in data extraction and 99.6% accuracy, but a 21% improvement in end-to-end processing time after integration with the bank's credit decisioning platform (Moody's CreditLens), plus an additional 9% from later AI features; analysts still conduct and validate spreads before submission.
population_and_setting: Anonymous top global bank, wholesale credit and lending team; >120 users
study_or_observation_method: Vendor narrative; method, baseline and period not reported
intervention_and_comparator: Automated spreading + integration with credit decisioning platform vs prior manual spreading
outcome_measured: Data extraction speed; accuracy; end-to-end spreading processing time
quantitative_result: '70% acceleration in extracting data'; 'accuracy rate of 99.6%'; '21% improvement' in end-to-end processing time; 'additional 9%' efficiency from Phase 3. No baselines or denominators.
limitations: Vendor marketing; anonymous client; no baseline, method or time period; headline stat blocks display '0 %'.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Shows the pattern expected in IC workflows: big gains on the mechanical extraction/reformatting step (W5) become much smaller end-to-end because validation and judgment remain. Needs verification with bank-authored or independent data.
analyst_inference: Even a favorable vendor source reports end-to-end gains (~21%) far below task-level gains (~70%); consistent with Fuster's ~20% end-to-end estimate. Treat as illustrative only.

proposition_tested: P1.3 Rework due to inaccurate/incomplete advisor output is a major driver of review; also P1.4 adaptation to recipient criteria
observed_finding: A lender's technology director states that independent engineer (IE) results taken alone are generally inadequate for structuring, so lenders underwrite conservatively using sensitivity cases, haircuts, parallel assessments and structural protections; downside cases must account for relevant uncertainties and P50 bias.
population_and_setting: US utility-scale solar project finance and tax equity; Wells Fargo REEF
study_or_observation_method: Conference presentation drawing on the lender's portfolio data and IE reports
outcome_measured: Lender's stated response to IE energy estimates
source_locator: Slide 8 ('All models are wrong, but some are useful...'), 'Theory vs. Practice' bullets
short_exact_excerpt: IE results in isolation are generally inadequate, leading to conservative underwriting (sensitivity cases, haircuts, parallel assessments, structural protections, etc.).
limitations: Stated view of one lender; does not quantify how much effort goes to parallel assessments versus haircuts; no transcript.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; directly on point: names four retained lender activities. 'Parallel assessments' is re-derivation (W1/W3); 'haircuts' and 'sensitivity cases' are adaptation to the lender's criteria informed by observed bias (W3/W4). Need to verify the share of each across lenders.
analyst_inference: The lender's stated reason for retained work is accuracy (P50 bias, too-narrow uncertainty), not lack of traceability. This points to W3/W4 more than W2. Better traceability alone would not remove haircuts tied to empirical bias. It might reduce the parallel-assessment component only if it exposes which assumptions drive bias.

proposition_tested: P1.3 inaccurate/incomplete advisor output drives review; P2.4 visibility into omitted uncertainty
observed_finding: The lender characterises IE 10-year P99:P50 ratios as inconsistent, not comprehensive and trending optimistic. It says empirical data show uncertainty distributions are too tight, that some uncertainty factors (availability, degradation) are commonly omitted, and that operational data show significant P50 bias beyond recent IE adjustments.
evidence_type: direct (buyer-side practitioner statement with portfolio data)
population_and_setting: Lender portfolio performance index of 32 solar projects, adjusted for curtailment and normalised to 99% availability
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of operating performance with IE-equivalent P-cases (charts)
intervention_and_comparator: Actual production vs IE P-cases
outcome_measured: Performance index vs IE P50/P99; IE 10-year P99:P50 ratios
quantitative_result: Chart labels on slide 7 read '~87%' and '~83-94% range' for IE 10-year P99:P50 ratios (precise meaning, i.e. central value vs spread, not stated in text); n=32 projects for performance index (slides 4-5); time period not stated
short_exact_excerpt: Operational data demonstrate significant P50 bias—beyond recent IE adjustments for sub-hourly clipping, complex terrain, and availability.
limitations: Chart values not extractable; selection of 32 projects unknown; lender has an interest in conservative assumptions.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; shows inconsistent uncertainty reporting across IEs ('not comprehensive') as well as bias.
analyst_inference: 'Not comprehensive' and 'commonly omitted' factors are X4 gaps: the lender cannot see which uncertainty components were considered. Standardised component-level uncertainty disclosure might reduce some reconstruction (W2). The P50 bias part is W3 and needs back-testing, not traceability.

proposition_tested: P1.4 Adaptation to recipient-specific policies/criteria is a major driver of retained work
observed_finding: The lender applies its own sizing rules to IE P-cases: debt coverage ratios on 1-year P99 (x1.0) and P50 (x~1.3), with P50 typically governing debt sizing; tax equity uses P50 for PTC forecasts and 10-year P99 as a structuring metric. Sizing parameters and commercial terms are largely set before detailed diligence.
population_and_setting: US solar debt and tax equity
outcome_measured: Use of IE outputs in sizing
quantitative_result: Debt: coverage on 1-year P99 x1.0 and P50 x~1.3
source_locator: Slide 3 ('Typical Application of Uncertainties for Solar Project Financing')
short_exact_excerpt: Sizing parameters and commercial terms largely established prior to detailed diligence
limitations: Typical-practice statement from one lender; coverage multiples vary by market and deal.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; shows the W4 step: IE P-values feed the lender's own coverage tests and tax-equity flip models.
analyst_inference: Because sizing is largely fixed before detailed IE diligence, the IE report may mostly confirm or adjust terms. Most of the lender's adaptation could be mechanical once P-cases and the uncertainty breakdown are available in structured form (W4/W5). Unverified.

proposition_tested: P-NEW: IE incentive structure (reputational, not financial, risk; sponsor engagement) gives lenders a rational reason to discount IE outputs (W3)
observed_finding: An IE managing director presents the IE role as an unbiased independent technical review, says results should be the same whichever party engages the firm, and notes the IE bears no direct financial risk, only reputational risk. Overly conservative modeling means developers won't engage; overly aggressive or inaccurate modeling means the industry will no longer accept the IE's work.
population_and_setting: US renewable IE practice (financing, tax equity, M&A)
short_exact_excerpt: No direct financial risk, instead, reputational risk
limitations: Supplier self-description; not evidence of actual bias.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; names the incentive tension that a lender would weigh.
analyst_inference: IEs are often sponsor-engaged (see R3C-S04) and face a 'developers won't engage' constraint. That makes lender discounting partly rational (W3) and partly governance (W1). Traceability tools do not change this incentive.

proposition_tested: P5.1 Repeatability rises with standardized evidence formats; P2.4 visibility into scope/uncertainty
observed_finding: The IE lists open issues: 'black box' uncertainty vs individual sources of error, the value of standardisation, inconsistent reporting of availability (contractual vs actual), and how to compare a project to peer data. It says IEs need operating data, standardisation of processes and standardisation of language to support apples-to-apples comparison.
population_and_setting: US renewable IE practice
short_exact_excerpt: “Black Box” uncertainty vs individual sources of error/uncertainty
limitations: Questions and stated needs, not measured effects.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; supplier confirms that a lack of standard uncertainty decomposition and definitions hampers comparison.
analyst_inference: Both buyer (E02) and supplier (E05) name non-standard, non-decomposed uncertainty reporting as a problem. That is the X4/W2 gap the thesis targets, though neither shows that fixing it reduces lender effort.

proposition_tested: P1.4 adaptation (here: sponsor adapting to the IE view); contextual on the economic stakes of P90
observed_finding: A developer describes keeping its 'build' model aligned with the IE's view. Across 20 case-study projects it reports an average of $70,000 of value per 1% increase in P90-1yr, and a 2.3% average P90-1yr gain from ground-tuned resource data. Higher P-values mean higher debt sizing.
population_and_setting: Lightsource bp, 20 solar projects (Americas)
study_or_observation_method: Internal comparison of tuned vs untuned resource data
intervention_and_comparator: Ground-tuned vs untuned satellite resource data
outcome_measured: P90-1yr and estimated value
quantitative_result: Average $70,000 per 1% increase in P90-1yr (independent of DC size); average +2.3% P90-1yr with tuned data; n=20 projects; in 2 cases P50 and P90 decreased
source_locator: Slides 3, 5, 7 ('The Evolution of the Model', 'What does Tuned Data Mean', 'By The Numbers')
short_exact_excerpt: Independent of DC size, we observed an average of $70,000 for every 1% increase in P90-1yr.
limitations: Self-reported; valuation method not given; sponsor incentive.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; shows that several parties (sponsor, IE, lender) keep their own energy models, and that small P90 differences are worth money, which motivates scrutiny.
analyst_inference: Parallel models exist on both sides of the deal. Duplication is structural, not only a lender habit. The money at stake per 1% of P90 helps explain why lenders retain parallel checks.

proposition_tested: P1.1 retained review driven by required independent judgment (here: what an IE scope actually contains)
observed_finding: In a filed technical due diligence report for a solar portfolio securitization, the IE describes reviewing the methodology behind the sponsor's energy production estimates. It does not describe running its own PVsyst simulation. It weather-adjusted the sponsor's expected energy using MERRA-2 GHI anomaly data, based uncertainty on review of pre-construction PVsyst reports and operating data, and found the financial-model energy yields generally reasonable.
population_and_setting: ~43.5 MWdc distributed solar portfolio (DSD), US, 2022 securitization
intervention_and_comparator: Weather-adjusted expected energy vs original expected energy
outcome_measured: Ratio of adjusted expected to original expected energy; estimated impact
quantitative_result: Portfolio weather-adjusted expected energy 98.7% of original expected (Table 4-1, as returned by fetch tool); estimated downward impact of 1.3% on weather-adjusted expected production (Section 4.2.1/1.5.3); 0.7% P90 portfolio-effect benefit (Section 1.5.3)
short_exact_excerpt: reviewed the methodology for DSD's energy production estimates
limitations: Fetch-tool extraction; truncated parts read in a second pass; whether B&V ran any independent model cannot be fully excluded; one deal.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; shows that at least some bankable IE work in securitization is review-and-adjust of the sponsor's EYA, not full independent re-derivation.
analyst_inference: This is a 'review' scope (the W2 setting): the IE checks sponsor methodology and adjusts with operating data. Better traceability of sponsor EYA inputs could plausibly lower that review cost. That is untested.

proposition_tested: P1.1 governance/reliance limits drive retained recipient work
observed_finding: The report states it was prepared solely for the sponsor's use and should not be relied upon by any other party. The IE's total liability is capped at the compensation received from the sponsor.
population_and_setting: Same securitization report
outcome_measured: Reliance/limitation terms
short_exact_excerpt: should not be relied upon by any other party
limitations: Typical boilerplate; investors may obtain reliance letters not visible here.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; no-reliance terms and liability caps leave investors, and rating agencies, with their own judgment burden.
analyst_inference: Limits on reliance are a structural W1 driver that persists whatever the transparency.

proposition_tested: P1.1 required independent judgment (does guidance require independent re-derivation or allow verification?)
observed_finding: IFC guidance says utility-scale projects should include a professional independent energy yield assessment 'produced and/or verified' by an experienced bank-grade consultant, at a confidence level of at least P75, if not P90.
population_and_setting: Utility-scale solar PV, emerging markets (IFC)
source_locator: Chapter 13 (Power Purchase Agreements), Section 13.2.1 text, printed p. 151
short_exact_excerpt: utility-scale projects should include a professional independent energy yield assessment, produced and/or verified by an experienced consultant with a track record of producing “bank grade” data, and a confidence interval of at least P75, if not P90.
limitations: Developer guide in a PPA context; not a lender requirement document.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; the DFI standard accepts either producing or verifying an EYA. Independent re-derivation is therefore not mandated by this guidance.
analyst_inference: 'Produced and/or verified' means verification-mode work (W2-type) is accepted as bankable in at least this DFI guidance. That leaves room for traceability to matter.

proposition_tested: P1.1 required independent judgment: lender technical due diligence includes yield prediction
observed_finding: IFC says investors and project-finance lenders will require technical due diligence that at minimum includes a site visit and 'solar resource assessment and energy yield prediction with uncertainty analysis'. Most other items are phrased as 'review' (design, technology, contracts, grid, permits, financial model inputs). The process requires the sponsor to put documentation in an online data room and ends with a technical due diligence report.
population_and_setting: Solar PV project financing (IFC guidance)
short_exact_excerpt: Solar resource assessment and energy yield prediction with uncertainty analysis.
limitations: Does not specify whether lender's advisor must re-run the model or may review the sponsor's; descriptive guidance.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; the minimum lender TDD lists energy yield as a prediction task alongside review tasks. Wording is ambiguous on independence.
analyst_inference: Together with E09, DFI guidance tolerates both modes. The W1/W2 split is therefore set deal by deal in the ToR, which public sources rarely show.

proposition_tested: P1.3 inaccurate advisor output drives review (rational discounting, W3)
observed_finding: Back-testing 115 pre-construction EYAs for 94 wind plants (6 owners, 19 named consultants) against 707 plant-years, the study finds P50s overestimate production. It says neither EYA uncertainty nor the P90 is conservative enough. It found no statistically significant difference across consultants.
population_and_setting: 94 wind plants, 6 countries (76 US), CODs mostly 2012-2017
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of EYA P50/P90 with long-term-corrected operational AEP
intervention_and_comparator: EYA predictions vs realised long-term-corrected production
outcome_measured: P50 bias; prediction-error SD vs stated EYA uncertainty; exceedance level of EYA P50
quantitative_result: P50 bias -7.4% to -6.6% (post-2010 CODs, by scenario) vs -6.7% to -5.5% in Lunacek et al. 2018. Prediction-error SD without IAV 11.4%-13.1% vs EYA long-term uncertainty 7.5% +/- 2.1%. EYA P50 sits at about P22 of the corrected distribution (SD 30 pp). Consultant ANOVA p = 0.7263.
short_exact_excerpt: neither the energy yield assessment uncertainty nor the P90 is conservative enough
limitations: Wind (not solar); owner-contributed sample; extracted via fetch tool.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; gives an empirical basis for lenders' haircuts and own downside cases on wind EYAs.
analyst_inference: Systematic bias shared across consultants (no significant consultant effect) suggests a second EYA by another consultant would not correct it. Back-test-based haircuts (W3/W4) would. This weakens the case that traceability removes discounting, but supports keeping structured EYA data for back-testing.

proposition_tested: P1.3 inaccurate/variable advisor output drives review; P2.4 component visibility
observed_finding: Comparing eight consultancies' estimates for 10 wind plants, consultants tended to overestimate gross energy and then compensated by overestimating losses. The mean P50 bias was near zero but plant-to-plant variability was significant, and disagreement between consultants stayed flat through the loss steps. Consultant differences could change LCOE by up to $10/MWh.
population_and_setting: 10 US wind plants; 8 consultancies
study_or_observation_method: Comparison of consultant gross-to-net estimates with operational data
intervention_and_comparator: Consultant estimates vs each other and vs operations
outcome_measured: P50 bias by loss step; inter-consultant spread; LCOE impact
quantitative_result: Mean P50 bias near zero; LCOE differences up to $10/MWh between consultants (abstract)
short_exact_excerpt: The disagreement between consultants, however, remains flat throughout the addition of losses.
limitations: Abstract only; small sample.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; inter-consultant dispersion is material, so a single IE number carries model risk. That rationalises parallel assessments or second opinions.
analyst_inference: Offsetting errors (gross too high, losses too high) are only visible with component-level disclosure (X4). A headline P50 can look right for the wrong reasons. This supports structured, decomposed reporting for detection, though no effort or detection outcome was measured.

proposition_tested: P1.3 inaccurate advisor output (bias) motivates discounting
observed_finding: DNV's validation of its own offshore energy assessments reports a slight negative bias in P50 predictions. Underperformance risk exceeds the chance of overperformance, partly attributed to curtailment, balancing payments and availability issues.
population_and_setting: Offshore wind projects assessed by DNV
intervention_and_comparator: Predicted vs actual
outcome_measured: P50 bias
short_exact_excerpt: The results show a slight negative bias in the prediction of P50 energy output
limitations: Summary only; magnitudes and n not seen; self-assessment.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; offshore wind; same mechanism.
analyst_inference: Even a leading consultant's self-validation shows a downside skew, which is consistent with lender haircuts.

proposition_tested: P5.1 standardization/accreditation increases comparability; context for parallel assessments
observed_finding: A vendor blog says yield uncertainty typically ranges 8% to 14%. It reports that in a DTU proficiency test on Walney 3 & 4, 28 participants' estimates had a standard deviation of about 3% but more than 10% between the most conservative and most optimistic results. It says ISO 17025 accreditation is increasingly referenced in lender technical advisor requirements, and that standards make results reproducible, traceable and comparable when applied rigorously.
evidence_type: vendor blog citing a proficiency test (second-hand)
population_and_setting: Wind yield assessment practice (Europe)
outcome_measured: Inter-participant spread
quantitative_result: DTU Walney 3&4 test: 28 participants; SD ~3%; >10% min-max difference (second-hand)
short_exact_excerpt: more than 10% difference between the most conservative and most optimistic results
limitations: Vendor marketing; original DTU test not retrieved; claims about lender TA requirements are unquantified.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; inter-consultant spread of this size gives a lender reason to want a second view. Accreditation is a lender-side requirement that standardises process, not content.
analyst_inference: Accreditation and standards target process comparability (P5.1). No evidence here that they reduce lender re-analysis.

proposition_tested: P1.4 adaptation to recipient's criteria (rating agency substitutes its own case); P1.3
observed_finding: According to a search-engine summary (article not accessed), S&P concluded that one-year P90 estimates are the best proxy for forecasting rated Spanish solar plants, and that one-year P50 and P75 estimates overstate future production for its rated portfolio.
population_and_setting: S&P-rated Spanish solar plants
limitations: Search summary only; must be verified before use.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; if confirmed, a rating agency replaces the IE P50 with its own more conservative base case derived from back-testing.
analyst_inference: Consistent with Fitch (already in the register): agencies adapt IE outputs to their own criteria, motivated by observed bias.

proposition_tested: P1.1 (what public lenders procure: 'independent engineer reviews')
observed_finding: According to a search-engine summary (PDF blocked), NY Green Bank's 2014 RFP for technical and engineering advisor services lists services 'as is common practice for a lender's engineer', including preparing independent engineer reviews for transaction due diligence.
population_and_setting: NY Green Bank, 2014
limitations: Unverified; does not show whether EYA re-derivation was required.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence itself; a public lender procures a standing lender's engineer to produce 'reviews'. The split between review and independent EYA is unknown.
analyst_inference: Weak; included as a lead.

proposition_tested: P1.1 required independent judgment vs P1.2 review of others' analysis (what an LTA scope requires for energy yield)
observed_finding: The development-finance lenders' LTA terms of reference frame energy-yield work as review and verification of the Sponsor's analyses. The LTA is to review the Sponsor's energy yield analyses and verify they are consistent with plant design and feedstock assumptions, considering supply, efficiency, technology, losses, availability projections, and uncertainties and deviations. It is also to review the Sponsor's probability-based production forecasts. No independent energy yield assessment is requested.
population_and_setting: 12.7 MW biogas/CHP project, Kenya; senior loan up to USD 50 million from EAIF, EDFI, BIO
outcome_measured: Specified LTA scope
source_locator: Section 'Feedstock Resource and Energy Yield Assessment', PDF p. 6
short_exact_excerpt: Review of the energy yield analyses undertaken by the Sponsor and verify that its results are consistent with the plant design and the feedstock supply assumptions.
limitations: Biogas rather than solar/wind; one RfP; a biogas yield depends on feedstock models that differ from irradiance/wind EYAs.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; a public DFI lender scope places LTA yield work in 'review of sponsor analysis' mode (W2 setting). Whether solar/wind LTA ToRs from DFIs use the same mode needs verification (the World Bank wind ToR was blocked).
analyst_inference: This is the clearest public example found of an LTA scope that is review, not re-derivation. Here, sponsor-side traceability (inputs, losses, uncertainty components) would directly affect LTA effort.

proposition_tested: P1.4 adaptation to lender criteria; P3.1 integration into lender analysis
observed_finding: The ToR asks the LTA to review technical inputs and work with the Lender in its analysis of the financial model, including running different scenarios. The LTA comments on the adequacy of technical assumptions (yield, availability, degradation, downtime, etc.) and proposes alternatives where inputs are inappropriate. Deliverables are a major-issues list within one week of the site visit, a draft report with professional opinions by area within three weeks, and an open-items list.
population_and_setting: Same as R3C-E17
outcome_measured: Specified LTA tasks and deliverables
quantitative_result: Major-issues list within 1 week of site visit; draft report within 3 weeks of site visit
source_locator: Sections 'Financial Model' (PDF p. 8) and 'List of Major Issues and Draft Report'
short_exact_excerpt: Review technical input assumptions and work with the Lender in their analysis of the financial model including running different scenarios on the financial model.
limitations: Intended scope only.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; the lender's own scenario analysis (W4) is procured as a joint LTA-lender task. Part of the adaptation work is therefore outsourced to the advisor rather than retained.
analyst_inference: The 'open items list' is a structured coverage artefact (X4-like) already built into practice. Integration with the lender model is explicitly in scope.

proposition_tested: P1.1 governance/reliance structure drives retained independent judgment
observed_finding: Each lender's decision to finance depends on satisfactory results of 'our respective due diligences' and internal approvals. The LTA report is prepared primarily for the Lenders and may be shared with equity and mezzanine investors only on a non-reliance basis.
population_and_setting: Same as R3C-E17
outcome_measured: Reliance terms
short_exact_excerpt: The LTA’s report will be prepared primarily for the Lenders but may be shared with the equity and mezzanine investors on a non-reliance basis.
limitations: Standard terms; does not show how much separate work each lender does.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; reliance and internal approval structures mean non-relying parties (equity, mezzanine) and each lender's credit function keep their own judgment duty.
analyst_inference: W1 persists structurally whatever the report's transparency. Transparency may change how cheaply that judgment is exercised, not whether it is required.

proposition_tested: P2.4 visibility into uncertainty / P5.1 standardization; P1.2 reconstruction from non-comparable outputs
observed_finding: IEA PVPS states there is no standardized uncertainty framework for lifetime PV yield predictions and a lack of definitions, which makes it difficult for financers and investors to compare uncertainty assessments. Commonly reported figures (initial yield and its P90, lifetime average and its P90) may not suffice for financial models covering degradation and inter-annual variation. It also reports that no respondent to its LTYP reporting questionnaire applied a physical soiling model in bankability studies; only estimated monthly averages were used.
population_and_setting: PV yield assessment practice (international)
study_or_observation_method: Literature/expert synthesis; LTYP reporting questionnaire (n not located)
short_exact_excerpt: Up to now, there is no standardized uncertainty framework for lifetime energy yield predictions available. Furthermore, there is a lack of definitions in this field
limitations: Authors' assessment as of 2018; does not measure financiers' effort.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; non-standard uncertainty reporting forces lenders to translate or re-derive P-cases for their own models.
analyst_inference: Translating non-standard uncertainty outputs into lender-specific P-cases is a mix of W2 (missing decomposition) and W4 (lender-specific cases). Standardisation could cut the W2 part.

proposition_tested: P1.1 vs P1.2 (when do investors require additional independent assessments?)
observed_finding: IEA PVPS characterises investor practice: investors typically require one yield assessment (YA); more may be requested if results are unclear, and multiple YAs can be averaged to set a purchase value. It asks why different assessors get different answers and whether one YA is more reliable.
population_and_setting: PV investment practice (international)
short_exact_excerpt: Typically, investors require one YA. In some cases, more YAs might be requested if results are unclear. The various YAs can be averaged to assign a purchase value to a given project.
limitations: Unsupported generalisation; no frequency data.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; suggests independent re-derivation (a second YA) is conditional, triggered by unclear results, rather than routine.
analyst_inference: If additional YAs are triggered by unclarity, clearer and more traceable YAs could reduce some duplicate assessments (a W2 mechanism). If triggered by inter-assessor dispersion (E22), clarity alone would not suffice.

proposition_tested: P1.3 inaccurate/variable advisor output; P2.4 visibility into assumptions enables reliability judgment
observed_finding: In a blind exercise, seven skilled yield assessors given the same detailed inputs produced different results. Differences were attributed mainly to modeler experience and assumptions: irradiance database and site adaptation, degradation, total modelling uncertainty, and soiling and shading. The authors recommend highlighting the assumptions and modelling chain and publishing post-mortem comparisons with measured data. They say they have identified the input and output data an assessor must provide for a YA's reliability to be judged.
population_and_setting: 7 independent yield assessors; PV systems at Bolzano (IT) and Alice Springs (AU)
study_or_observation_method: Same-input blind yield assessments compared with each other and with measured yield
intervention_and_comparator: Assessor vs assessor; predictions vs measured
outcome_measured: P50/P90 ranges; SD of initial YA; measured yield
quantitative_result: Bolzano: P50 1095-1406 kWh/kWp; P90 997-1274 kWh/kWp; mean initial YA 1278 kWh/kWp, SD 9.7%; LTYP-implied 2010-2019 average 1253 vs measured 1275 kWh/kWp. Alice Springs: P50 1757-1985; P90 1631-1819 kWh/kWp; mean 1878, SD 3.9%; measured initial 2075 and 10-year average 1926 kWh/kWp.
short_exact_excerpt: differences in these stem primarily from personal experience and assumptions by the modeler
limitations: n=7 assessors, 2 sites; summary only; assessor selection not described.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; a single IE P50 embeds assessor-specific judgment, which rationalises lender sensitivities and parallel views. The recommended remedy is assumption and modelling-chain visibility.
analyst_inference: This is the strongest source linking X4 (assumption visibility) to the ability to judge which assessment to trust. It shows a mechanism and a recommendation, not an effort or detection outcome.

proposition_tested: P1.4 adaptation to recipient's own criteria (rating agency); P1.3 discounting based on observed performance
observed_finding: Fitch takes the third-party experts' energy yield forecast (P50/one-year P90 spread of 18%) as an input to its volume-risk assessment ('Weaker'). It then applies its own 7% production haircut in both base and rating cases, citing moderately volatile actual load factors in FY19-FY20. Base case is P50 generation with the 7% haircut; rating case is one-year P90 with the 7% haircut. Separately, it notes the operating cost forecast is not validated by an independent technical advisor and stresses it by 15% in the rating case.
evidence_type: direct (rating-agency application of criteria to an IE/third-party forecast)
population_and_setting: ReNew Power Restricted Group 4, Indian wind and solar portfolio; USD notes, 2021
outcome_measured: Agency base/rating case construction
quantitative_result: Third-party P50/one-year P90 spread 18%; Fitch production haircut 7% (base and rating cases); 15% opex stress in rating case; refinancing rate 11% in base case
source_locator: Key rating drivers / Fitch's key assumptions sections (as reproduced)
short_exact_excerpt: Hence, we apply a lower haircut of 7% on the volume forecast in our base and rating cases.
limitations: Secondary reproduction; one transaction; the reason the haircut is 'lower' (vs what reference) was not fully visible.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Target workflow is renewable-energy investment/credit diligence; shows the W4 pattern at a rating agency: the IE forecast is accepted as the base input and then haircut by agency-specific rules informed by observed operations. Where an independent advisor has not validated an input, the agency stresses it.
analyst_inference: The agency does not re-derive the EYA. It adapts it (haircuts, P-case choice) and applies heavier stress where independent validation is missing. That is consistent with 'review + adapt' rather than 're-run', at least at rating agencies.

proposition_tested: P2.2 Structured evidence/checklists preserve or improve detection of material errors (tested via a standard fraud-risk checklist used in audit planning)
observed_finding: Auditors using a standard risk checklist structured by SAS No. 82 risk categories made lower fraud risk assessments than auditors without a checklist in an SEC enforcement fraud case; the authors interpret this as a less effective diagnosis of the fraud.
population_and_setting: 69 practicing auditors; US; SEC enforcement fraud case
study_or_observation_method: Between-subjects 2x2 experiment (checklist vs none; standard program vs none)
intervention_and_comparator: Standard SAS No. 82 risk checklist vs no checklist
outcome_measured: Fraud risk assessment level in a known-fraud case
quantitative_result: not reported in abstract (direction only)
short_exact_excerpt: auditors who used a standard risk checklist, structured by SAS No. 82 risk categories, made lower risk assessments than those without a checklist.
limitations: Single case; abstract only; effect sizes not seen; checklist is an internal tool, not a coverage disclosure from a producer.
transferability_to_target_workflow: Mechanism: a standardized list handed to a reviewer shapes what the reviewer looks for. In diligence, a lender's or IC's own checklist / an advisor's 'scope of work' table could play this role.
